title: Senses in action: how long a signal takes, and how the brain guesses

summary.text: A friend drops a ruler between your fingers without warning. You grab it, but never before it has fallen a hand-length. Light from the falling ruler reached your eye almost at once, so where did the delay happen? Your child times a signal on its way from eye, ear and skin to the hand, then asks how big a change must be before a sense notices, why a smell fades while you stand in it, and why you cannot tickle yourself. Along the way you meet pain that arrives in two waves, a rubber hand that starts to feel like yours, and animals that sense magnetic fields and electricity. Nobody yet knows how a brain makes one steady 'now' out of signals that all arrive late.
summary.art: A child's hand catching a falling ruler between thumb and finger, with a glowing line of sparks running from the child's eye up to the brain and down the arm to the hand.

intro.hook: Ask a friend to hold a ruler upright, with its bottom between your finger and thumb. Do not move. Your friend lets go without any warning. Close your fingers as fast as you can. Look at the number where you caught it. Did your fingers close at once?
intro.text: They did not. The ruler fell a hand-length or so before you caught it, even though you saw it start to fall. In this unit you measure that delay for the eyes, the ears and the skin, and you find out where the time goes. Then you test how small a change a sense can notice, how a smell fades while you stand in it, and how your brain guesses what is about to happen. You also meet animals that sense magnetism and electricity.
intro.art: A ruler dropping between a child's open finger and thumb, with a friend's hand above it, in a bright kitchen.

outcomes: I can explain that every sense sends the brain tiny pulses, and that a stronger stimulus makes more pulses each second, not bigger pulses.
I can measure my reaction time with a falling ruler, compare sight, sound and touch, and explain where the time is spent between sensing and moving.
I can explain that nerve signals travel at different speeds, and use that to explain why a stubbed toe hurts in two waves.
I can explain what a threshold is, and use a fair test to show that the smallest change a sense notices depends on how much was there to start with.
I can explain why a steady smell, touch or sight fades from notice, and why that helps a body.
I can explain that the brain keeps a map of the body, that pain is made by the brain as a warning, and why people can feel a limb that is gone.
I can give evidence that the brain predicts what it is about to sense, and use it to explain why you cannot tickle yourself.
I can give examples of animals with senses that humans lack, and say which questions about the senses scientists still cannot answer.

terms.meaning: Anything that a receptor can notice, such as light, a sound, a touch, a smell or a change in warmth. The plural is stimuli.
terms.example: The smell of tadka in hot oil is a stimulus for the smell receptors in your nose.
terms.art: A pan of sizzling tadka with little arrows of smell going towards a child's nose.

terms.meaning: A nerve cell. It has branches that gather messages, a body, and a long thread that sends the message on. Nerves are bundles of these threads.
terms.example: Some neurons in a grown-up's leg are about one metre long, from the toe to the lower back.
terms.art: A single nerve cell with branches at one end and a very long thread at the other, drawn along a leg.

terms.meaning: A tiny wave of electricity that travels along a neuron. Every pulse is the same size. A stronger stimulus makes more pulses each second, not bigger ones.
terms.example: A light touch might send 10 pulses each second. A hard press might send 100.
terms.art: Two rows of identical sparks along a nerve thread: a few sparks for a light touch, many sparks for a hard press.

terms.meaning: A fatty wrapping around some nerve threads, like the plastic around an electric wire. Pulses move much faster along wrapped threads.
terms.example: Touch and muscle signals travel along wrapped threads. Slow, dull pain travels along unwrapped ones.
terms.art: A nerve thread with white fatty sleeves along it, and a spark jumping from gap to gap.

terms.meaning: The time between a stimulus and your response to it. It includes the signal going in, a decision in the brain, and the signal going out to the muscles.
terms.example: When a ruler starts to fall, your reaction time is the time until your fingers close. For most people it is about one fifth of a second.
terms.art: A stopwatch beside a falling ruler and a child's closing fingers, with three little arrows: in, decide, out.

terms.meaning: The smallest amount of a stimulus that a sense can notice. Anything smaller goes unnoticed.
terms.example: A very faint tick of a wall clock in a quiet room is at your threshold for hearing.
terms.art: A staircase with a step labelled 'noticed' and a step below it labelled 'not noticed', and a faint clock tick on the lower step.

terms.meaning: The smallest change in a stimulus that you can tell apart. Scientists often shorten it to JND. A small JND means a sharp sense.
terms.example: Two bags of rice weigh 500 grams and 540 grams. If you can just tell which is heavier, 40 grams is your JND at that weight.
terms.art: Two cloth bags in a child's two hands, one slightly lower than the other, with a small label of the weight difference.

terms.meaning: When a sense gets used to a stimulus that stays the same, and stops signalling it so strongly. Receptors do this on their own.
terms.example: When you walk into a kitchen full of frying onions, the smell is strong. After a few minutes you hardly notice it.
terms.art: A child in a kitchen with a big cloud of smell around her, shrinking cloud by cloud in three panels.

terms.meaning: A feeling the brain makes to warn you that something may be harming your body. Nerve endings in the skin and body send danger signals, and the brain decides how much it hurts.
terms.example: A thorn in your foot makes the foot hurt. The warning is made in your brain.
terms.art: A foot with a thorn, a nerve thread up the leg, and a brain at the top with a red warning light.

terms.meaning: Your brain has a strip on its surface where each part of your body has its own patch. Parts with many receptors, such as lips and fingertips, get big patches.
terms.example: On the brain's body map, your thumb takes more room than your whole back.
terms.art: A strip of brain with a drawing of a body spread along it, with giant lips, hands and tongue and a tiny back.

terms.meaning: The feeling that an arm or a leg is still there after it has been lost. The brain's patch for that limb is still working.
terms.example: Many people who lose a hand can still feel their fingers itch.
terms.art: A person with one sleeve empty, and a faint glowing outline of a hand where the arm used to be.

terms.meaning: A guess about what will happen next. Your brain makes predictions about what you are about to sense, so it can react faster and ignore what it expected.
terms.example: When you reach for a door you know, your brain predicts how heavy it feels. A door that is much lighter than expected makes you stumble.
terms.art: A child's brain with a thought bubble showing a heavy door, while the real door swings open lightly.

terms.meaning: Something that your senses and brain build wrongly, even though the signals from the senses were correct. You can know it is wrong and still sense it.
terms.example: In the rubber hand test, a glove on the table starts to feel like your own hand.
terms.art: A rubber glove on a table next to a hidden real hand, with two brushes stroking both together.

terms.meaning: Linking one sense with another. People link sounds with shapes, or tastes with colours, in ways that are much the same across the world.
terms.example: Most people say the made-up word 'bouba' fits a round shape and 'kiki' fits a spiky one.
terms.art: A round blobby shape and a spiky star shape, with the words 'bouba' and 'kiki' floating by them.

terms.meaning: Sensing magnetic fields. Some birds, turtles, fish and insects can sense the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.
terms.example: A small bird flying south for the winter may use the Earth's magnetism to keep going the right way.
terms.art: A small bird flying over hills with faint lines of the Earth's magnetic field curving around the bird.

terms.meaning: Sensing weak electric fields. All living muscles make tiny electric fields, so a hunter with this sense can find hidden prey.
terms.example: A shark has jelly-filled pores on their snout that sense the weak electricity of a fish hidden in the sand.
terms.art: A shark gliding over sand, with faint electric rings rising from a buried flatfish.

explanations.concept: A signal is a pulse, and a strong signal is a fast drumbeat of pulses
explanations.definition: A nerve pulse is a tiny wave of electricity that runs along a neuron. All pulses are the same size. A stronger stimulus makes more pulses each second.
explanations.description: In the earlier unit on the senses you learned that every sense sends the brain nerve signals. Now look closer at one signal. A neuron is a nerve cell with a long thread. When the neuron is stirred, tiny gates open in the skin of the thread. Charged particles rush in, and that makes a small wave of electricity that runs down the thread. This wave is a nerve pulse. A pulse is like a spark that is either there or not there. It is never half a spark, and it is never a bigger spark. So how does the brain know that a touch is hard and not gentle? In 1926 two scientists, Edgar Adrian and Yngve Zotterman, listened to a single nerve thread from a frog's muscle. When they hung a heavier weight on the muscle, the pulses did not get bigger. They came faster. A light weight gave a few pulses each second. A heavy weight gave many. Edgar Adrian later shared the 1932 Nobel Prize for this kind of work. So the strength of a sense is written in the speed of the drumbeat. What the signal is about is written in which thread it travels along, as you learned before. Your brain holds about 86 billion neurons. Suzana Herculano-Houzel, a Brazilian scientist, counted them in 2009 by turning a brain into a soup of cell centres and counting those. Each eye sends about one million threads to the brain, and every thread sends its own drumbeat. Plants also use pulses. A Venus flytrap has trigger hairs inside her trap. One touch on a hair sends one pulse, and nothing happens. A second touch within about 20 seconds makes the trap snap shut. She counts.
examples: Press a fingertip on a table very lightly, then harder. The skin sends the same kind of pulse both times. The harder press only sends more of them each second.
A Venus flytrap shuts only when two touches arrive within about 20 seconds. A raindrop that touches one hair once does not trigger her. She uses pulses to tell prey from rain.
Doctors can record the pulses from a nerve and play them as clicks. A stronger touch sounds like faster clicking.
explanations.art: Three nerve threads side by side with rows of identical sparks: few sparks for a light touch, more for a firmer touch, and a crowd of sparks for a hard press, with a brain at the end of each.
explanations.context: This card looks closely at what a single nerve signal is, and how the brain can tell a weak stimulus from a strong one.

explanations.concept: Fast wires and slow wires: why signals take time
explanations.definition: Nerve pulses travel at different speeds. Threads wrapped in myelin carry pulses fastest, up to about 100 metres each second. Thin unwrapped threads carry pulses at about 1 metre each second.
explanations.description: Light from a falling ruler reaches your eye almost at once. But your finger does not close at once. The signal has to be made in the eye, travel to the brain, be sorted and decided on, and then travel down the arm to the muscles. How fast is a nerve signal? In the 1840s the German scientist Johannes Müller wrote that its speed would probably never be measured, because it must be too fast. In 1850 another German scientist, Hermann von Helmholtz, proved him wrong. He gave a frog's leg nerve a small shock in two places, one near the muscle and one further away. The muscle twitched a little later when the shock was further away. From the extra time and the extra distance, Helmholtz worked out the speed: about 30 metres each second. That is much slower than light, and slower than a car on a highway. Later scientists found that different threads have different speeds. The big threads wrapped in myelin, which carry touch and the position of muscles, run at 50 to 100 metres each second. Threads for sharp pain are thinner and run at about 5 to 30 metres each second. Threads for slow, dull pain are thin and unwrapped, and run at about 1 metre each second. This explains something you may have felt. Stub your toe, and first comes a quick sharp pain. About a second later comes a slow, deep ache. Two kinds of thread, two speeds. From toe to brain is about 1.5 metres for a grown-up. At 1 metre each second that is about a second and a half. At 15 metres each second it is only a tenth of a second. On top of travel time, the brain needs time to decide. In total, simple reaction times are about 0.15 to 0.25 seconds. Touch and hearing are usually a little faster than sight, because the eye does extra work before it sends its signal. In a race, sprinters wait for the sound of a gun, not for a flash. The rule says that if a runner starts less than 0.1 seconds after the gun, the start was too early. Nobody can truly react that fast, so the runner must have guessed.
examples: Stub your toe and count. The sharp pain comes first and the dull ache comes after, because the two kinds of pain travel along threads of different speeds.

In 1796 an English astronomer, Nevil Maskelyne, dismissed his assistant David Kinnebrook, because Kinnebrook timed a star crossing about 0.8 seconds later than Maskelyne. Years later, the German astronomer Friedrich Bessel found that every astronomer has their own delay. It is called the personal equation.
A sprinter's feet cannot leave the block less than 0.1 seconds after the gun without the start counting as a false start.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a child's body from eye and toe up to the brain, with a fast thread drawn as a thick wrapped wire and a slow thread drawn as a thin string, and a stopwatch on each.
explanations.context: A nerve signal is fast but not instant. This card explains how long it takes, why a stubbed toe hurts twice, and why every reaction has a delay.

explanations.concept: The faintest thing a sense can notice: thresholds
explanations.definition: A threshold is the smallest amount of a stimulus that a sense can notice. Below it, you notice nothing. Above it, you notice. Thresholds change with the person, the place and how carefully they pay attention.
explanations.description: Every sense has a faintest stimulus that it can pick up. In 1942 Selig Hecht, a scientist in the USA, and his team asked people to sit in a completely dark room for about half an hour. This lets the eyes become as sensitive as they can. Then they showed very faint flashes of light. They worked out that a person can notice a flash when only a handful of light particles are caught by the light cells of the eye, fewer than 15. On a very dark clear night, scientists have estimated that your eye could notice a candle flame tens of kilometres away. The threshold for smell is also very low. Cooking gas has no smell of its own. Gas companies add a smelly chemical so that a leak is noticed even when there is very little in the air. Hearing tests in a clinic work by finding your threshold. The tester plays softer and softer beeps and finds the softest one you can hear. Here is a surprise. A threshold is not one fixed line. In the 1950s scientists such as Wilson Tanner and John Swets showed that a person's answer depends on two things. One is how well the sense works. The other is how ready the person is to say yes. A careful person who does not want to be fooled says no to faint signals. An eager person says yes more often. At the very faint end, the same person can answer differently on different days. A tired nose, a noisy room or a worried mind can all change a threshold. The best tests ask many times and then look for the stimulus that you notice about half of the time.
examples: A hearing test finds the softest beep each ear can notice.
Cooking gas is given a strong smell on purpose, so even a tiny leak is above most people's threshold.
In a noisy market you miss a soft sound that you would hear easily in a quiet room. The noise raises your threshold.
explanations.art: A dark room with a child sitting with eyes adapted, a very faint small light across the room, and a ladder of light brightness steps with one step marked 'just noticed'.
explanations.context: How small can a stimulus be before you notice it? This card explains thresholds, and why they are not as fixed as they sound.

explanations.concept: Ratios, not amounts: how big a change must be to notice it
explanations.definition: The smallest change you can notice, called the just noticeable difference, is usually a fixed fraction of what was there to start with. This is called Weber's law.
explanations.description: Lift a light bag in one hand and a slightly heavier bag in the other. You can tell which is heavier. Now carry a very heavy sack in each hand, and make one a little heavier. You cannot tell, unless the difference is bigger. In the 1830s a German scientist, Ernst Weber, tested this with people lifting weights. He found that the change needed to notice a difference was not a fixed number of grams. It was a fixed fraction of the weight you started with. In careful lab tests, about 2 or 3 extra grams in every 100 grams could be noticed. At home with bottles, most people need a bigger step, often 10 in every 100 or more. The same idea works for other senses. A candle is easy to see in a dark room and impossible to see in bright sunshine, because the same candle is a tiny fraction of the sunlight. A whisper is clear in a quiet room and lost in a noisy market. In 1860 Gustav Fechner, another German scientist, turned Weber's finding into a rule about how sensations grow. When a stimulus doubles, a sensation grows by a small, equal step. This is why we measure many things on a scale where each step multiplies. Loudness is measured in decibels, and every 10 decibels means 10 times more sound energy, yet it sounds only about twice as loud. Astronomers grade the brightness of stars in magnitudes. The ancient Greek astronomer Hipparchus sorted stars into six classes. In 1856 Norman Pogson showed that one class step is about 2.5 times in brightness, so five steps is 100 times. Working with ratios lets the eye work from dim starlight to bright noon sunshine, a range of billions of times, without getting dazzled. Weber's law is only approximate. It works best in the middle of the range and fails near the threshold and near the top.
examples: If you can just tell 100 grams from 110 grams, then at 500 grams you might need about 550 grams to just tell the difference. The fraction stays about the same.
A torch is easy to spot at night and almost invisible at noon. It is the same torch, but a tiny fraction of the daylight.
A decibel scale makes a whisper (about 30 decibels) and a loud horn (about 110 decibels) fit on one short ruler.
explanations.art: Two pairs of bags: a small pair where one bag is slightly bigger and a big pair where the difference is the same size but cannot be noticed, with a ladder of ratios beside them.
explanations.context: How big does a change have to be before you notice it? This card explains why the answer depends on how much was there to start with.

explanations.concept: Tired receptors: why steady things fade
explanations.definition: Adaptation is when a sense reports a steady stimulus less and less. It saves effort, keeps the sense ready for change, and works at the receptor itself and also in the brain.
explanations.description: Walk into a kitchen where onions are frying and the smell is strong. After a few minutes you hardly notice it. Walk outside for a while and come back, and the smell is strong again. This is adaptation. Smell receptors send a burst of pulses at the start, then fewer and fewer if the smell stays the same. Vision adapts too. When you walk from sunshine into a dark cinema, you see nothing at first. The light cells in the eye need time to become sensitive again. Cones recover in a few minutes. Rods take about 20 to 30 minutes to become fully ready. Then a torch in the same hall can look blinding. Even a steady picture fades. Your eyes make tiny jumps several times each second, even when you think you are staring. In 1953 Lorrin Riggs and his team fixed a tiny mirror to a contact lens, so that a picture moved exactly with the eye and stayed in the same place on the retina. The picture faded to nothing within seconds. Scientists now think that the eyes must keep moving for us to keep seeing. Adaptation is not a fault. It means that your senses spend their effort on what changes, and a change is the thing that matters most. A new smell in the house, a new sound in the night, a new touch on your arm may all mean something. But not all senses adapt equally. Pain adapts much less than smell does. A warning that faded away while you were still being hurt would not be much use. This is also why a smell that you cannot notice may still be there. A gas leak or a slowly rotting food may have been in the room for hours. A person who has just arrived can smell it at once.
examples: You stop noticing your own house's smell, but a visitor notices it as soon as they walk in.
Walking into a dark cinema hall, you cannot see the seats. After 10 minutes you can see the whole room, because your rods have become ready.
A watch on your wrist feels like nothing after a minute, but you notice at once if you take it off.
explanations.art: Three panels of a child in a kitchen with a cloud of onion smell that shrinks, and a visitor at the door with a surprised nose, and a graph line of pulses falling off.
explanations.context: Why do you stop noticing a smell after a while? This card explains why steady things fade, and why that is useful.

explanations.concept: The body map in the brain, and pain that the brain makes
explanations.definition: The brain has a strip on its surface with a patch for each part of the body. Pain is a warning that the brain makes from danger signals. It is not a direct reading of damage.
explanations.description: In the 1930s and 1940s, a Canadian brain surgeon, Wilder Penfield, operated on awake patients who had a serious illness called epilepsy. The brain itself has no pain nerves, so patients can stay awake while the surgeon works, with just the scalp numbed. When Penfield touched a spot on the strip of brain with a tiny electric probe, the patient said that they felt a touch on a body part, for example a thumb or a lip. He joined the spots into a map of the body on the brain. The map is strange. The hands, the lips and the tongue take up huge areas, and the back and legs take up small ones. Parts with many receptors get the most room. This fits the two-point test you may have done earlier. Pain also comes from nerve endings that warn of danger, called nociceptors. But the feeling of hurting is made in the brain. A person born with a broken gene for a certain sodium gate in the pain nerves feels no pain at all. In 2006 a team led by James Cox and Geoffrey Woods found this gene in families in Pakistan. These people hurt themselves badly without knowing, because they never get the warning. The map also explains phantom limbs. In the 1870s an American doctor, Silas Weir Mitchell, described soldiers who still felt a limb that had been lost. Most people who lose a limb feel it. The brain's patch for the hand is still there and still active. In the 1990s V. S. Ramachandran, a neuroscientist who grew up in India, and Diane Rogers-Ramachandran reported that some patients felt touches on their face as touches on the missing hand, because the face patch lies next to the hand patch. They also built a mirror box that makes it look as if the missing hand is back. For some patients, this eased their phantom pain. Heart trouble can show up as pain in the left arm. The nerves of the heart and the arm share paths into the brain, which can mix up the message.
examples: A map of the body drawn the size of the brain's patches has giant lips, hands and tongue and a tiny back.
A person who has lost a hand may feel a touch on their cheek as a touch on the missing fingers.
A person who feels no pain can break a bone and walk on it for days without knowing.
explanations.art: A strip of brain with a drawn body spread along it so the lips, tongue and hands are enormous and the back and legs are tiny, beside a normal child's outline.
explanations.context: Where in the body do touch and pain really happen? This card shows that the brain keeps a map of your body, and that pain is made by the brain.

explanations.concept: The brain guesses ahead: why you cannot tickle yourself
explanations.definition: The brain predicts what you are about to sense, especially from your own movements. It treats what it predicted as less important. That is why your own touch does not tickle.
explanations.description: Try to tickle your own palm. It does not work. Someone else can tickle you easily. In 1998 Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith tested this with a machine. People held a soft piece of foam that was moved by a robot arm. When they moved a handle to make the foam stroke their own palm, the touch felt less ticklish than when the machine did the same stroke without their control. When the scientists added a small delay between the movement and the touch, the touch tickled more. So the brain predicts the result of your own movement, and turns down the feeling that it expected. This is a general trick. Your eyes jump from point to point about three times each second. The picture on the retina smears each time, but you never see the smear, because the brain turns off the signal during each jump. A trick shows this. Look in a mirror at your left eye, and then at your right eye. You never see your eyes move. The brain also guesses what things should look like. In 2001 a team found that when you glance at a clock with a second hand, the first second seems to last longer than the others. The brain fills in the gap during the eye jump with what it sees next. Predictions can also lead you wrong. In 1998 Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen showed that, if you cannot see your real hand, and a rubber hand on a table is stroked in time with your hidden hand, you start to feel the rubber hand as yours. Your brain finds the best match for the signals and decides that the hand you can see is your hand. Many scientists now think that perception is mostly prediction, checked and corrected by signals from the senses. How far this idea goes is still being tested.
examples: You cannot tickle yourself, but a friend can. Your brain expects your own touch.
Walk down a step that is not there in the dark. You stumble, because your brain had predicted the step and your foot did not find it.
In the rubber hand test, brushes on a hidden hand and a rubber hand, in time with each other, make many people feel the rubber hand as part of them.
explanations.art: A child touching her own palm with a feather, with a faded copy of the touch inside her brain cancelling it out, and a friend tickling her with a bright spark of signal.
explanations.context: Your brain does not wait for signals. This card shows how it guesses ahead, and explains why you cannot tickle yourself.

explanations.concept: Rewired and cross-wired: senses are less separate than they seem
explanations.definition: Parts of the brain are not fixed to one sense. They can learn to handle signals from another sense, and the senses link up in surprising ways.
explanations.description: In the earlier unit you learned that signals from the eye and the ear look much alike. If so, can the brain use a part of itself for a different sense? Since the 1980s, Mriganka Sur, an Indian-born brain scientist in the USA, and his team rerouted the eye nerves of newborn ferrets so they reached the part of the brain that normally listens to sound. In the experiments reported in 2000 by Laurie von Melchner, Sarah Pallas and Mriganka Sur, the ferrets could still respond to light with that rewired part. The part of the brain that usually hears had learned to work with signals from the eye. In the 1960s Paul Bach-y-Rita, a doctor in the USA, built a chair with 400 small vibrating points against the back. A camera sent a picture to the points. After practice, blind people learned to tell shapes and even to catch a rolling ball. Later versions put the pattern on the tongue. The senses also link up in ways that happen on their own. In 1929 the German psychologist Wolfgang Köhler showed people two shapes, one round and one spiky. He asked which one is called 'takete' and which is called 'baluba'. Most chose round for baluba. In 2001 V. S. Ramachandran and Edward Hubbard repeated this with the words 'bouba' and 'kiki', in the USA and with Tamil speakers in India, and found the same pattern in both groups. Tests across many languages find that most people match the sounds to the shapes in the same way. Babies only a few months old do it too. About 1 person in 25 has synaesthesia, which means that one sense always triggers another. For example, they may always see the letter A as red. Scientists do not yet know why the links exist, but one idea is that the brain finds patterns that are shared between senses.
examples: A blind person using a tongue display can learn to tell the shape of a cup without touching it.
Most people choose 'bouba' for the round shape and 'kiki' for the spiky one, whichever language they speak.
A person with synaesthesia may taste a flavour when they hear a certain word.
explanations.art: A ferret's brain with the eye nerve redirected into the hearing area, beside a round shape labelled 'bouba' and a spiky star labelled 'kiki'.
explanations.context: Are the senses locked in separate boxes? This card shows how the brain can be rewired, and how senses link up in surprising ways.

explanations.concept: Senses we do not have: magnetism, electricity and heat
explanations.definition: Many animals have receptors for things humans have no receptor for, such as the Earth's magnetic field, weak electric fields and infrared heat.
explanations.description: The Earth is a giant magnet, and its field is always around us. In the 1960s two German scientists, Wolfgang and Roswitha Wiltschko, showed that European robins kept in cages tried to head in the direction of their migration, but only when the magnetic field around them matched the real one. When they turned the field with coils, the robins turned too. Scientists think that some birds sense the field through a special molecule in their eyes, and that the field changes how a chemical reaction in that molecule goes. This idea is still being tested. Sea turtles also seem to use the field. Olive ridley turtles nest on the beaches of Odisha and Tamil Nadu. Scientists think that they, like other sea turtles, may use the field to find their way back across the sea, but this has been tested more in other kinds of sea turtle. Electric fields are even more surprising. Every living muscle makes a tiny electric field when it moves. A shark has jelly-filled pores on her snout, called the ampullae of Lorenzini, after the Italian who described them in 1678. They can feel the field of a fish buried in the sand. The platypus has thousands of electric sensors in her bill, and hunts with her eyes shut. In 2013 a team led by Daniel Clarke and Heather Whitney found that bumblebees can sense the weak electric field around a flower. A flower that has just been visited has a changed field, which may tell a bee that the nectar is gone. Pit vipers sense infrared, or heat, with small pits between their eyes and nostrils. Some other animals have extra kinds of light receptor. The mantis shrimp has 12 to 16 kinds, compared with our three. But in tests, she was not better at telling similar colours apart, so more kinds of receptor do not always mean finer sight. Each animal's senses are built for the life that animal lives.
examples: A shark can sense the weak electricity of a flatfish hidden under sand.
Bumblebees can sense the electric field of a flower before they land on it.
A mantis shrimp has up to 16 kinds of light receptor, but was not better than other animals at telling colours apart.
explanations.art: A shark above sand with faint electric rings from a buried fish, a robin with magnetic field lines and a snake with a glowing warm mouse seen as heat.
explanations.context: Some animals sense things that humans have no receptors for. This card shows magnetism, electricity and heat, and how scientists found out.

explanations.concept: Is there a real world behind the signals?
explanations.description: Each sense gives the brain a stream of pulses. The brain turns them into a world of colours, sounds, smells and a steady 'now'. The signals arrive late, are different from animal to animal, and are filled in by guesses. So scientists and philosophers ask: how much of what you experience is the world, and how much is built by you? Everyone agrees that there is a world, that light really reaches your eye and that molecules really reach your nose. The argument is about what the experience is, and whether the world itself looks anything like it.
examples: The same fruit is red to a child and appears dark to a bee in ordinary light. Each is right about what their eyes detect.
A person who has lost a hand feels the hand, even though nothing is there. The feeling was real. The hand was not.

perspectives.who: Direct realists, many philosophers and ordinary people
perspectives.explanation: When you look at a mango, you see the mango itself. The delay of a fifth of a second is small and does not change what you see. Signals are the means by which we meet the world, not a curtain in front of it.

perspectives.who: Anil Seth, a neuroscientist in England, and others who study the predicting brain
perspectives.explanation: The brain never meets the world directly. It makes a best guess about the causes of its signals and corrects the guess. Seth calls what we experience a 'controlled hallucination', controlled because the senses keep checking it.

perspectives.who: Donald Hoffman, a scientist in the USA, in 2015
perspectives.explanation: Evolution shaped our senses to help us survive, not to show us the truth. Like icons on a phone screen, our colours and shapes hide what is really there. Many scientists think this goes too far, because accurate senses usually help survival.

perspectives.who: Advaita Vedanta, an Indian school of thought, and Adi Shankara of about the 8th century
perspectives.explanation: The world of shapes and colours that the senses show is appearance. What is real beneath it is one awareness. The science of the senses does not prove this, but it shows how much of our world is built by us.

explanations.art: A mango on a table, with three different drawings of it from three viewers: a child in full colour, a bee in ultraviolet patterns and a snake in heat, and a question mark in the middle.
explanations.context: After following every sense down to nerve pulses, this card asks the big question: how much of the world we experience is really out there, and how much is built by the brain?

agreed.text: Every nerve pulse is the same size. The strength of a stimulus is written in how many pulses arrive each second.
agreed.evidence: Since the 1920s, scientists have recorded single nerve threads in frogs, cats and people. A harder press, a brighter light or a louder sound always gives faster pulses, never bigger ones.

agreed.text: Nerve signals take time. Simple reaction times are about 0.15 to 0.25 seconds, and nerve pulses travel at speeds from about 1 to about 100 metres each second.
agreed.evidence: Hermann von Helmholtz measured the speed of a frog nerve in 1850. Reaction times have been timed in millions of people since, with the same range of answers.

chart.title: How fast a nerve signal travels along different threads (about)
chart.note: Numbers are rounded. Speeds vary from person to person and thread to thread.

agreed.text: The smallest change you can notice is roughly a fixed fraction of what was there before, for weight, loudness and brightness. This is called Weber's law, and it works best in the middle of the range.
agreed.evidence: Ernst Weber tested people lifting weights in the 1830s. Later tests with sound and light found much the same pattern, with some exceptions near the faintest and strongest stimuli.

agreed.text: A steady stimulus is reported less and less. Receptors adapt, and so does the brain, which saves effort and keeps the senses ready for change.
agreed.evidence: Recordings from smell, touch and light receptors show their pulses falling away when the stimulus stays the same. A picture that is held perfectly still on the retina fades within seconds.

agreed.text: The brain keeps a map of the body, and pain is made by the brain as a warning. It is not a direct reading of damage.
agreed.evidence: Touching spots on an awake patient's brain made them feel touches on parts of their body. People with a broken pain-nerve gene feel no pain. People who have lost a limb often feel the limb for years.

agreed.text: The brain predicts what its own movements will cause, and turns down those expected signals. That is why your own touch does not tickle.
agreed.evidence: In 1998 Sarah-Jayne Blakemore and her team found that a touch you make yourself feels less ticklish than the same touch made by a machine, and more ticklish if a small delay is added.

challenging.claim: You see and hear things at the very moment they happen.
challenging.who: Most people in daily life, and many old books about the mind
challenging.for: Everything seems to happen at once. When a ball hits a wall, the sight and the thump seem to come together.
challenging.against: Every signal needs time to travel along nerves, and the brain needs more time to sort it. Reaction times show a delay of about a fifth of a second. The brain also adjusts the timing so that sight and sound seem to match.
challenging.context: This card is about the common feeling that you sense the world at the very instant it happens.

challenging.claim: Pain is a direct measure of how much your body is damaged.
challenging.who: A common belief, held by many people and in many old books
challenging.for: A big cut usually hurts more than a small scratch, so pain and damage seem to go together.
challenging.against: Soldiers with bad wounds have sometimes felt almost nothing in the moment. A paper cut can hurt a lot. People with phantom limbs feel pain from a limb that is gone. The brain makes pain from danger signals, memory and the situation.
challenging.context: This card is about whether pain just reports how badly you are hurt.

challenging.claim: You are born with the senses you have, and they cannot get much better.
challenging.for: Receptors are made by the body, and nobody can add a new kind of receptor by practice.
challenging.against: Practice changes the brain's use of the signals. Tea tasters in Assam, Darjeeling and the Nilgiris train for years to tell tiny differences between leaves. Perfumers and musicians do the same in their own senses. The receptors are the same, but the brain's reading gets finer.
challenging.context: This card is about whether practice can make a sense sharper.

challenging.claim: Humans have no sense of the Earth's magnetic field.
challenging.who: Most scientists today, and many books
challenging.for: No one has found a human magnetic organ. No person has been shown to use the field to find their way.
challenging.against: In 2019 a team led by Connie Wang and Joseph Kirschvink reported that some people's brain waves changed when the magnetic field around them was turned in a certain way. The people did not notice anything, and other scientists want the test repeated.
challenging.context: This card is about whether people, like some birds and turtles, can sense magnetism without knowing it.

challenging.claim: An animal with more kinds of colour receptor sees finer colours.
challenging.who: A common assumption after the mantis shrimp's receptors were counted
challenging.for: The mantis shrimp has 12 to 16 kinds of receptor, and we have three. It seems that more should mean more colours.
challenging.against: In 2014 a team led by Hanne Thoen tested mantis shrimps and found that they could not tell close colours apart as well as people can. Maybe they read colour in a quick, simple way.
challenging.context: This card is about whether more kinds of receptor always means better sight.

big_questions.q: Your 'now' is built from signals that are already about a fifth of a second old. Do you ever live in the present?
big_questions.hint: Think of the falling ruler. Then think of starlight that left a star long ago.

big_questions.q: Your senses are best at noticing change. What would the world feel like if nothing ever changed?
big_questions.hint: Think of a smell that fades, and a watch you forget you are wearing.

big_questions.q: Pain is made in the brain, but it feels like it is in your toe. So where is the pain?
big_questions.hint: Think of a person who feels an itch in a hand that is gone.

big_questions.q: If the brain is always guessing, how can it tell when a guess is wrong?
big_questions.hint: Think of stumbling on a step that was not there, or a rubber hand that stops feeling like yours.

big_questions.q: Should a sense show what is true, or what is useful? A bee's colours help her find flowers. Are they true?
big_questions.hint: Think of a fruit that is red to you and dark to a bee. Which one is the real fruit?

big_questions.q: A shark feels the electricity of a hidden fish. Is electricity part of the shark's world only, or is it in our world too, where we cannot notice it?
big_questions.hint: Think of what a robin does with the Earth's magnetism, which is all around you right now.

big_questions.q: Scientists tried a belt that buzzes towards north. After weeks, wearers said their sense of space had changed. If you gained a new sense, would you be the same person?
big_questions.hint: Think about how a sense becomes part of how you think, not only part of what you detect.

big_questions.q: Maskelyne sent away an assistant for timing a star 0.8 seconds later than him. Who was right, and how could they have found out?
big_questions.hint: Think of how each person's reaction time is different, and how you could measure it.

story.title: The Honest First Minute
story.note: Devika, Saraswathi Ammamma, Mr. Balaji and the warehouse are made up. Mattancherry in Kochi really is an old spice-trading quarter. The science in the story is real. A smell that stays the same fades from notice, and the nose recovers after a few minutes in fresh air. Damp black pepper really can grow mould.
text: Devika went to her grandmother's spice warehouse every day after school. It stood in Mattancherry, near the old harbour in Kochi, in a lane where the air always smelled of pepper, dried ginger and sea salt.

Her grandmother, Saraswathi Ammamma, had run the warehouse for forty years. People said she had the best nose in Kochi. She could sniff a handful of cardamom and tell you which hill it came from. Traders drove all the way from Coimbatore just to ask her opinion.

On this Thursday a lorry stood outside the door. Forty sacks of black pepper had to be loaded by six o'clock for a buyer from Coimbatore, Mr. Balaji. He was a large, impatient man who kept tapping his watch.
'Everything is checked,' said Ammamma, wiping her hands on her sari. She had been inside since six that morning, weighing sacks, sniffing samples and scolding the boys who carried them. 'Load them.'
Devika dropped her school bag by the door. At once, her nose wrinkled.
'Ammamma,' she said, 'something smells wrong in here.'
'It smells of pepper,' said Ammamma. 'This is a pepper warehouse.'
'Not only pepper. There is another smell underneath. It is like a wet towel that someone forgot in a bag.'

Mr. Balaji snorted. 'A child's imagination, madam. I am a busy man.' Ammamma lifted her chin and breathed in, long and slow. She frowned. She smelled pepper, and nothing else. 'My nose is never wrong,' she said, a little sharply.

Devika's heart thumped. She did not want to say that her grandmother's nose was wrong. But she remembered something from science class that week. 'Ammamma, when I come out of the kitchen after Amma has fried onions, I cannot smell the onions any more. My teacher says the nose stops reporting a smell that stays the same. It only wakes up when something changes.'
'You have been standing in this smell since six o'clock this morning,' she went on, very quietly. 'I have been in it for one minute. My nose is awake. Yours is tired.'

Nobody in forty years had dared to say such a thing to Saraswathi Ammamma. Mr. Balaji began to laugh, and then stopped, because Ammamma did not. She was thinking. 'Come,' she said to Devika at last. 'We will test it. Mr. Balaji, you will have tea, and it is my treat.'

They walked out to the tea stall by the water. The breeze smelled of fish, diesel, hot tea and the jasmine in a passing woman's hair. Ammamma drank slowly, with her eyes half closed. Devika watched the clock on her wrist. Ten whole minutes passed.

Then they walked back to the warehouse. At the door, Ammamma stopped. Her eyes opened wide. 'Ah,' she whispered. Under the sharp, hot smell of pepper, there was a thin, cold, musty smell. It had been there all afternoon. She had simply stopped hearing it.

She followed it to the back corner by the wall. That morning's monsoon shower had leaked through a crack in the roof. Three sacks at the bottom were wet through. Pepper that stays damp grows mould within days, and mould spreads. A whole lorryload could have been ruined before it reached Coimbatore.

Mr. Balaji went pale. 'Those three would have gone on my lorry,' he said slowly. The boys carried the wet sacks into the sun to dry. The other thirty-seven were loaded, and the lorry left at half past six, with Mr. Balaji waving from the window.

That evening Ammamma sat on a stool and looked at Devika for a long time. 'Why did your nose find it, and mine did not?' she asked. 'Mine did not stop working. It was only tired of the same smell,' she added to herself, as if she were learning it by heart.

'From today,' she said, 'there are two rules in this warehouse. Before any lorry leaves, a nose that has just come in from outside sniffs the sacks first. And whoever has been inside all day goes out to the tea stall for ten minutes before deciding anything.'

'And who is the fresh nose?' asked Devika, trying not to smile. 'I come at four every day.' Ammamma laughed for the first time that evening. 'Then you are hired. Your wages are one packet of banana chips.' And that is how a girl of nine became the Honest First Minute of the best spice warehouse in Kochi.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a smell that stays the same fades from notice. Smell receptors send a burst of pulses at the start, then fewer and fewer. Ammamma's nose was not broken. It was tired of the pepper, which had been constant since morning. A change, like a new damp smell, is exactly what a nose reports, but only a nose that has been away or just arrived. The ten minutes at the tea stall gave her receptors time to recover, so the first sniff back was honest. Devika's fresh nose was the first honest nose of the day.
ask: Why could Devika smell the damp when her grandmother could not?
Why did going to the tea stall help Ammamma's nose?
Name something in your own home that you can no longer notice, but a visitor could.
Why might a nose that fades on steady smells still be good to have?
How could you test whether a nose has become tired of a smell?

roots.context: We have followed the senses from stimulus to nerve pulse to brain, and found that everything arrives late, and arrives as pulses. Now we ask what this says about who is sensing, and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your fingers closed on the ruler about a fifth of a second after it began to fall. The light reached your eye almost at once. The delay happened inside you. So everything you sense has already happened, and your 'now' is built from slightly old signals.
deep_truth.habit: We think we meet the world as it is at this very moment. Every sense needs time to turn the world into pulses, carry them and sort them, so we live a little behind it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Ruler Drop test, the ruler fell about 15 to 20 centimetres before your fingers closed. At the speed a ruler falls, that is about 0.17 to 0.2 seconds.

three.who_am_i: The 'you' who is aware of this moment is always a fraction of a second behind the world, and you still feel that you are right here.
three.what_is_life: A Venus flytrap counts two touches before she shuts. A robin senses the Earth's magnetism. Every living being turns the world into pulses, then acts on them.
three.what_is_this_world: A light, a sound and a smell are very different in the world. Inside a body, all three become the same kind of pulse. The world we know is made where the world meets a body.

roots.thread: Light, sound, smell and pressure are very different things out in the world. Once they pass through a sense they are all the same: pulses on a thread. A bee, a shark and a child each turn the same world into different pulses, and each is right about what they detect. The world and the body that senses it are not two separate things. Each experience is made from both together, and made a moment late. If everything is one awareness, then the sensing is that awareness meeting itself, slowly, through many different bodies.

teachings.teaching: The Upanishad asks what is behind the senses. It speaks of the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind and the eye of the eye. Something hears through the ear and sees through the eye, and cannot itself be heard or seen.
teachings.link: Science finds that the ear and the eye only send pulses to the brain. The question of who is aware of those pulses is the same question the Upanishad asks.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that what we can know as 'the all' is the eye and what it sees, the ear and what it hears, the nose, the tongue, the body and the mind, each with what it meets.
teachings.link: This matches what the science of the senses finds. All we know of the world has come through the senses and the brain's work on their signals.

teachings.teaching: Plato, a Greek thinker, told of prisoners who see only shadows on a wall and take them for the whole of reality. One prisoner turns round and learns that the shadows were made by something else.
teachings.link: Our brain also meets the world through signals and builds a picture. The picture is useful and real as an experience, and it is not the thing itself.

science.text: Every sense turns the world into nerve pulses of the same size, and every signal takes time to arrive.
Perception is mostly the brain's prediction, corrected by the senses. Scientists argue about how far this idea goes.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India, and many modern philosophers called direct realists
other_view.view: Perception is the surest way of knowing. What you see and touch is simply there, and talk of a hidden world behind the senses is not needed. A delay of a fifth of a second does not stop you meeting the real mango.

practice.title: Catch the sound that has already happened
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Breathe in slowly three times. Now listen. Every time you notice a sound, whisper the word 'now'. Then ask yourself something. When you whispered, was the sound already finished? Keep listening for one minute, and notice how each sound arrives just after it was made.
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Listen for a minute. Whisper 'now' at each sound. Was the sound already over?

ask: If your 'now' is always a little late, what do you mean when you say 'right now'?
Who is the one that notices the pulses? Is it the eye, the brain, or something else?
If a bee, a shark and a child each meet the same fruit with different pulses, is there a fruit that is none of theirs?
roots.art: A child sitting still with closed eyes, with a ripple of sound reaching her ear and a faint ghost of the same child a moment ahead of her.

how_we_found_out.story: For centuries, people thought that a signal in a nerve must be as quick as thought, perhaps as quick as light. In the 1840s the famous German scientist Johannes Müller wrote that its speed would probably never be measured. In 1850 another German scientist, Hermann von Helmholtz, tried anyway. He took the leg nerve of a frog, with the calf muscle still attached. He gave the nerve a small electric shock at two spots, one near the muscle and one further away. Then he timed, with a fast device he built himself, how long the muscle took to twitch. The twitch came slightly later when the shock was further from the muscle. From the extra distance and the extra time, he worked out the speed. It was about 30 metres each second, much slower than light. Helmholtz soon tried it on people, who were asked to press a button when they felt a touch. The results varied more, but they showed the same thing. A signal takes time, and the body is always a little behind the world.
how_we_found_out.who: Hermann von Helmholtz, a German scientist (1821 to 1894)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists, including Johannes Müller, thought a nerve signal was too fast to measure, perhaps as fast as light. Helmholtz showed it is slow enough to time with a frog's leg.

games.title: Sense Detectives: why did that happen?
games.context: This is a detective game. Each card tells a short story about a sense doing something odd. You decide which of five ideas explains it, and then say why.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile on a table and ten tokens in five pairs, each token with a different idea written on it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A reader holding up one card and three players each putting a token face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card aloud. Everyone puts a token face down.

setup.art: Tokens turned over together, and the reader turning the card to read the answer on the back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back. Score a point for the right idea.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a short story about a sense on the front, and the idea that explains it on the back

items.f: Meena puts on a new watch. For the first minute she feels it on her wrist. By lunch she has forgotten it is there.
items.b: ADAPTING RECEPTORS. Touch receptors send fewer pulses when the pressure stays the same.

items.f: Arun jumps into a cool pond. At first it feels very cold. After five minutes it feels fine.
items.b: ADAPTING RECEPTORS. Temperature receptors adapt to a steady temperature and report the change.

items.f: A visitor walks into Kavya's home and says it smells strongly of mustard oil. Kavya has never noticed.
items.b: ADAPTING RECEPTORS. Her smell receptors have been in that smell for years and have faded it.

items.f: Farah walks into a dark cinema hall and sees nothing. Ten minutes later she can see all the seats.
items.b: ADAPTING RECEPTORS. The light cells in her eyes slowly became more sensitive in the dark.

items.f: Ravi stares at a dot on a page without moving his eyes. The faint grey shapes at the side of the page fade away.
items.b: ADAPTING RECEPTORS. A picture held still on the retina fades, because the eye needs change.

items.f: A candle is bright and clear at night. At noon in sunshine you cannot see its light.
items.b: TOO SMALL A CHANGE. The candle is a tiny fraction of the sunlight, so it adds a change too small to notice.

items.f: Farah can feel the difference when 20 grams is added to a 200 gram bag. Adding 20 grams to a 2 kilogram sack, she feels nothing.
items.b: TOO SMALL A CHANGE. The change you can notice is a fraction of what was there. 20 grams is one tenth of 200 grams and only one hundredth of 2000.

items.f: A whisper is easy to hear in a quiet library. At a loud wedding you cannot hear it at all.
items.b: TOO SMALL A CHANGE. The noise raises the amount of sound you need to notice anything new.

items.f: A mosquito whines near Lakshmi at night. She only hears it when the fan is switched off.
items.b: TOO SMALL A CHANGE. The mosquito's sound is a tiny change on top of the fan's noise.

items.f: A pinch of salt in a big pot of rasam makes no difference to the taste. The same pinch in a spoon of water tastes very salty.
items.b: TOO SMALL A CHANGE. The same pinch is a small fraction of the pot and a large fraction of the spoon.

items.f: Kavya tries to tickle her own foot with a feather. Nothing happens. Her brother does it, and she giggles.
items.b: THE BRAIN GUESSES. The brain predicts the touch from her own movement and turns down the feeling.

items.f: Mohan walks down the stairs in the dark. He thinks there is one more step, and his foot slams into the floor.
items.b: THE BRAIN GUESSES. His brain predicted a step that was not there, so the landing was a surprise.

items.f: Divya lifts a big box that she thinks is full of books. It is empty, and her arm flies up.
items.b: THE BRAIN GUESSES. Her brain predicted a heavy box and sent too much push.

items.f: A rubber hand and your hidden hand are stroked together with brushes. After two minutes the rubber hand starts to feel like yours.
items.b: THE BRAIN GUESSES. The brain finds the best match for the signals and decides the hand it can see is yours.

items.f: Sneha glances at a clock. The first second seems to last longer than the next ones.
items.b: THE BRAIN GUESSES. During the eye's jump the brain fills the gap with what it sees next, so that second seems longer.

items.f: A ruler is dropped between your fingers. You catch it after it has fallen a hand-length.
items.b: SIGNALS TAKE TIME. The signal goes from the eye to the brain, then to the hand. That takes about a fifth of a second.

items.f: Nandini stubs her toe. First she feels a sharp pain. A second later she feels a slow, deep ache.
items.b: SIGNALS TAKE TIME. Sharp pain travels on fast threads, and the dull ache on slow ones.

items.f: A sprinter starts 0.05 seconds after the starting gun. The judges say it was a false start.
items.b: SIGNALS TAKE TIME. Nobody can react that fast, so the runner must have guessed the gun.

items.f: In 1796 an astronomer sent away his helper, who timed a star crossing 0.8 seconds later than he did. Later, every astronomer was found to have their own delay.
items.b: SIGNALS TAKE TIME. Each person has their own delay between seeing and recording.

items.f: A fast bowler's ball takes about half a second to reach the bat. A batter's reaction time is about a fifth of a second.
items.b: SIGNALS TAKE TIME. The batter must start to move before the ball has been fully seen.

items.f: Newborn ferrets had their eye nerves joined to the hearing part of the brain. They still reacted to light.
items.b: A FLEXIBLE BRAIN. The part of the brain that usually hears learned to work with signals from the eyes.

items.f: A blind person wears a patch on the tongue connected to a camera. With practice, they can tell the shape of a cup.
items.b: A FLEXIBLE BRAIN. The brain learns to read touch signals from the tongue as a picture.

items.f: A person who has lost a hand feels a touch on their cheek as a touch on their missing fingers.
items.b: A FLEXIBLE BRAIN. The brain's cheek patch lies next to the hand patch, and the cheek signals spread into it.

items.f: A person born blind reads Braille with their fingers. A scan shows the brain's seeing part is busy.
items.b: A FLEXIBLE BRAIN. The seeing part of the brain learned to help with touch.

printables.title: 10 tokens: two for each of the five ideas

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 10 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Each player needs five tokens, one for each idea. The sheet has two sets. With more than two players, write the five ideas on small slips of paper.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. They pick the idea that they think explains the story.
Everyone turns their token over together. Then the reader reads the back aloud.
A player who picked the right idea scores 1 point. A player who also says the reason in one sentence, in their own words, scores 1 more.
The next player becomes the reader. Keep going until the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: you are the reader and the player. Read the front, put the token on the table, say your reason out loud, then read the back. Try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Read the five ideas on the tokens aloud once. No printer? Write the five ideas on paper slips. Read the cards from the screen.
flow.say: We have five ideas that explain odd things your senses do. Adapting receptors. Too small a change. The brain guesses. Signals take time. A flexible brain. Each story fits one idea.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Read the five ideas.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sense Detectives. You set up the game and meet the five ideas.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down a token. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who got a point, and who can give a reason?
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the stories that fit 'adapting receptors' have in common?
good: Something stayed the same for a long time.
The feeling faded.
The sense stopped reporting it.

flow.parent: Players often mix up 'adapting receptors' and 'too small a change'. In the first, a steady thing fades. In the second, something new is added but is too small next to what is already there.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how scoring works.

flow.do: Play the next six cards. When a player picks the wrong token, ask them to say which story clue made them choose it.
flow.say: A wrong token is useful. Which clue in the story made you choose it? Let us find the clue that points to the other idea.
flow.kid: Play six more cards. If you were wrong, find the clue you missed.

ask.q: How can you tell 'the brain guesses' from 'signals take time'?
good: In 'the brain guesses', the brain expected something before it came.
In 'signals take time', there is a wait between the event and the sense.
Both use the brain, but one is about expecting and one is about waiting.

flow.context: In this step, you play more cards and learn to use clues in the story to choose.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards. Keep score on the score sheet. Skip the reasons if time is short and score only the right idea.
flow.say: Now the last twelve. Keep your score. Remember to say why in one sentence.
flow.kid: Play the last twelve cards. Write down your score.

check.q: A story says that a person can smell a leak in the kitchen at once when they come in, but the cook cannot. Which idea fits best?
options: Adapting receptors
Signals take time
A flexible brain
check.why: The cook has been in the smell for hours, so the receptors send fewer pulses. The newcomer's receptors are fresh. Choosing 'signals take time' mixes up a fading smell with a delay.

flow.context: In this step, you finish the cards and keep your score.

flow.do: Add up the scores. Ask each player which idea they found hardest, and which story surprised them most.
flow.say: Add up your scores. Which idea was hardest for you? Which story surprised you most? What story could you make up for that idea?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Make up your own story for one idea.

ask.q: Can you invent a new story for one of the five ideas?
good: Something that fits 'adapting receptors', like a smell that fades.
A story with a clear clue.
A story where the sense changes over time.

flow.context: This is the last step of Sense Detectives. You count points and invent your own story.

experiments.title: Ruler Drop: how long does a signal take?
experiments.question: When a friend drops a ruler, how far does it fall before you catch it? Is the distance the same when you see it start to fall, hear a word, or feel a tap?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will you catch the ruler soonest by seeing it, hearing a word or feeling a tap? Which will be slowest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same ruler, the same catcher and the same hand every time. The catcher's thumb and finger start at the 0 centimetre end, with the ruler hanging between them. The dropper waits a different time before each drop, so the catcher cannot guess. Each cue is tried 3 times as practice and then 7 times for the record. The rounds are done in one order, and then in the opposite order after the two people swap roles, so that tiredness or practice does not favour one cue. Only the cue changes, so any difference comes from the cue. With 2 to 4 children, give three jobs: catcher, dropper and recorder. Rotate so each child is the catcher once, and give each catcher their own table. Two catchers fit in 45 minutes, so let the others catch in a second sitting.

materials.item: a light 30 centimetre plastic or wooden ruler, not a steel one
a table with a flat edge, or a chair with a flat arm, to rest the catching arm on
a second person to drop the ruler, and later to catch it
a pencil and paper for the results table, with 7 rows and 3 columns
a calculator or paper, to find the middle value

experiments.safety: Use a light ruler, so a miss does not hurt anyone's foot. The catcher sits down. Do not throw the ruler. Take a short break if your eyes feel tired. Do not use a steel ruler.

schedule.what: Guess. Set up. Do the seeing, hearing and touch rounds. Swap roles and repeat in the opposite order. Find the middle value and write your claim.

experiments.record: For each cue, write the seven counted catch distances. Cross out the three practice tries. Then find the middle value of the seven. Draw a bar for each cue using its middle value.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out how far a ruler falls before you catch it, when you are told it is falling by sight, by sound and by touch.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the middle catch distance for each cue
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers may be different. Sight is often slightly slower, but your results may not show it.

setup.art: A child sitting with an arm resting on a table edge and the thumb and finger open, with a ruler hanging between them and its 0 end level with the top of the thumb.
setup.caption: 1. The catcher rests an arm on the table. The ruler hangs between thumb and finger, with 0 at the top of the thumb.

setup.art: The catcher watching the ruler closely while the dropper holds it by the top end, ready to let go.
setup.caption: 2. Seeing round: the catcher watches the ruler. The dropper lets go at a surprise time.

setup.art: The catcher with eyes shut while the dropper says the word 'now' at the same moment as letting go.
setup.caption: 3. Hearing round: the catcher shuts their eyes. The dropper says 'now' as they let go.

setup.art: The catcher with eyes shut while the dropper taps their shoulder with the free hand at the same moment as letting go.
setup.caption: 4. Touch round: the catcher shuts their eyes. The dropper taps their shoulder as they let go.

setup.art: A close-up of the ruler caught in the fingers, with a finger-sized pointer showing the number at the top of the thumb.
setup.caption: 5. Read the number at the top of the thumb. Write it down.

flow.do: Show your child the ruler. Explain the three rounds. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both at the top of the results table.
flow.say: A friend will drop this ruler, and you will catch it. In one round you will watch it, in one you will hear a word, and in one you will feel a tap. Which will let you catch it soonest? Which will be slowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A friend drops a ruler. You catch it. You can see, hear or feel the cue. Which is fastest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that cue will be the quickest?
good: Seeing is quickest, because the eye is quick.
Touch is quickest, because the tap is on the body.
I do not know, so I will find out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Most children say that seeing will be quickest. Write the guess down, because the result may surprise them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ruler Drop test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Sit the catcher at a table. Rest their arm on the edge with the hand hanging over. The dropper holds the ruler by the 30 centimetre end. The 0 centimetre end is level with the top of the catcher's thumb. Do three practice drops with sight.
flow.say: Rest your arm on the table. Open your thumb and finger like a pair of tongs. Keep the ruler between them, not touching. I will let go without warning, and you grab. These first three tries are practice.
flow.kid: Rest your arm. Hold your fingers open. Catch the ruler when it drops. Three practice tries.
flow.parent: The ruler must hang freely, not touching the fingers. If the catcher can feel the ruler, they will catch it too quickly. The 0 mark is level with the top of the thumb, not the bottom. Practice tries do not count.

check.q: Why does the dropper wait a different time before each drop?
options: So the catcher cannot guess when it will drop
So the ruler falls faster
So the game is slower
check.why: If the drop came at the same moment each time, the catcher could guess and catch early. That would measure guessing, not the time the signal takes. A wrong pick about speed mixes up the ruler with the catcher.

flow.context: In this step, you set up and do three practice drops. These do not count.

flow.do: Do the seeing round. The catcher watches the ruler. The dropper counts silently to a number between 2 and 6, then lets go. Write the number at the top of the thumb for seven counted tries.
flow.say: Watch the ruler, not my fingers. I will let go when I choose. Catch it as fast as you can. Look at the number, and I will write it down.
flow.kid: Watch the ruler. Catch it as fast as you can. Say the number you caught.
flow.parent: Change the silent count each time. If the ruler falls out of reach, write 30 and say 'missed'. Do not measure with the ruler held at an angle.
flow.context: In this step, you do the seeing round and write down seven catch distances.

flow.do: Do the hearing round and then the touch round, with the catcher's eyes shut. For hearing, the dropper says 'now' as they let go. For touch, the dropper taps the catcher's shoulder as they let go. Do three practice tries and seven counted tries for each.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. In this round, I will say 'now' at the moment I let go. Catch as fast as you can. In the next round, I will tap your shoulder instead.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Catch when you hear 'now'. Then catch when you feel a tap.
flow.parent: The dropper must let go at the same moment as the word or the tap. A small mismatch is the same every time, so it does not spoil the comparison. If the dropper has trouble doing both, practise first.
flow.context: In this step, you do the hearing round and the touch round with the eyes shut.

flow.do: Swap places. The new catcher does the rounds in the opposite order: touch, then hearing, then seeing. Write seven counted tries for each.
flow.say: Now swap. The catcher becomes the dropper. This time we start with touch, then hearing, then seeing. That way, tiredness or practice cannot help one cue more than another.
flow.kid: Swap places. Do touch first, then hearing, then seeing.

check.q: Why do we do the rounds in the opposite order after swapping?
options: So practice or tiredness does not favour one cue
So the second person has a harder test
So the ruler stays new
check.why: If every catcher did seeing first, the cue done last would get the most practice or the most tiredness. Reversing the order balances this out, so the cue is the only thing that differs.

flow.context: In this step, the two people swap roles and the order of the rounds is reversed.

flow.do: For each cue, put the seven numbers in order and pick the middle one. Look at the three middle numbers. Ask your child for their claim, their evidence and their reasoning before you explain anything.
flow.say: Put the seven numbers for each cue in order, smallest to biggest. The middle one is the one to use. Which cue gave the shortest distance? What is your claim? What is your evidence? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Put each set of seven in order. Pick the middle one. Which cue was fastest? Why?

ask.q: Which cue gave the shortest catch distance, and does it match your guess?
good: Touch or hearing was quickest and seeing was slowest.
They were all about the same, so the cue did not matter much.
My guess was wrong, and I can say why I think so.

ask.q: Light travels almost instantly. So where was the time spent?
good: In the eye, the nerve and the brain.
In deciding to catch.
In the signal going down the arm to the hand.

flow.parent: Typical results (not promised): a middle value of about 12 to 22 centimetres for each cue, which is a fifth of a second or less. Touch and hearing are often 1 to 3 centimetres shorter than seeing, but luck can hide it. If the cues look the same, say so. That is a real result. Do not explain the cards yet. Let your child say where they think the time went. A guide to time: 5 cm is 0.10 seconds, 10 cm is 0.14, 15 cm is 0.17, 20 cm is 0.20, 25 cm is 0.23, and 30 cm is 0.25 seconds.

check.q: Why do we use the middle value of seven tries and not the biggest or smallest?
options: One lucky or sleepy try cannot change the middle value much
The middle value is always the correct one
The biggest value is too hard to read
check.why: A single try can be unusually quick or slow. The middle value stays steady even when one try is odd. It is not always 'correct', but it is more trustworthy than one extreme.

flow.context: In this step, you find the middle value for each cue and decide what your results say.

experiments.title: The Bottle Lift: how big must a change be to feel it?
experiments.question: How much heavier must a bottle be before you can tell which is heavier? Is the answer the same for a light bottle and for a heavy one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will you need the same extra water for a heavy bottle as for a light bottle, or more, or less? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the bottles are the same kind, closed, and with the water hidden. The lifter is blindfolded, and lifts one bottle in each hand. The helper puts the heavier bottle in a random hand each time. Each comparison is tried 4 times. The light set has a standard bottle of 100 millilitres and the heavy set has a standard of 400 millilitres. The extra water in each comparison bottle is the same fraction in both sets. Only the weight of the standard changes, so any difference comes from that. With 2 to 4 children, one is the lifter, one fills and keeps the key, and one writes right or wrong. Swap jobs for each set. Each lifter has their own results table, because every hand is different.
results_table: Smallest extra that I always got right (millilitres)
That extra as a share of the standard (out of 100)

materials.item: 6 identical plastic bottles with caps, each holding 1 litre
a measuring cup or jug with millilitre marks (a kitchen cup, or the cap-cup of a syrup or detergent bottle if it has ml marks)
water from the tap
a dupatta or soft cloth, folded, as a blindfold
small pieces of sticky tape and a pencil, to put a secret letter on the base of each bottle
a towel for spills, and a paper to write the results table

experiments.safety: Fill the bottles at the sink and wipe up any spills at once, because a wet floor is slippery. The lifter sits down while blindfolded.

schedule.what: Guess. Fill the light set and test it. Empty, refill for the heavy set and test it. Work out the share and write your claim.

experiments.record: For each set, write the smallest extra water that the lifter always got right. Then work out the extra as a share of the standard, out of 100. Compare the two shares.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find the smallest extra weight that you can feel, once for a light bottle and once for a heavy one.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the extra water needed to feel a difference
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers may be different. In the example, the heavy set needs 4 times as much extra water, which is the same share of the standard.

setup.art: Six identical bottles in a row on a counter being filled with different amounts of water from a measuring jug, with a small tape letter on each base.
setup.caption: 1. Fill six bottles: one standard and five comparison bottles. Put a secret letter on each base.

setup.art: A blindfolded child sitting down and holding two closed bottles, one in each hand, while a helper watches.
setup.caption: 2. The blindfolded lifter holds the standard in one hand and a comparison bottle in the other.

setup.art: The lifter pointing to one hand and saying 'this one', with the helper writing right or wrong in a table.
setup.caption: 3. The lifter says which hand is heavier. The helper writes right or wrong.

setup.art: The same six bottles being emptied and refilled with larger amounts of water for the heavy set.
setup.caption: 4. Empty the bottles and fill them again for the heavy set.

flow.do: Show your child the bottles and the jug. Say that you will find the smallest extra weight they can feel, for a light bottle and for a heavy one. Write their guess and their reason.
flow.say: I will put some water in six bottles. We will find how much extra water a bottle needs before you can tell it is heavier. We will do it for a light bottle, and then for a heavy one. Will the heavy one need the same extra, more or less? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How much extra water can you feel? Is it the same for a heavy bottle? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think a heavy bottle needs a bigger or smaller extra?
good: A heavy bottle needs more extra, because a small bit gets lost in a big weight.
It will be the same, because my hand is the same.
I think it needs less, because my arm works harder.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write it at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle Lift test. You guess before you test.
