flow.do: Fill the first bottle with 100 millilitres of water. Fill five more with 110, 120, 130, 140 and 160 millilitres. Put a secret letter on each base. Write which letter is which on the helper's paper. Close all the caps tightly.
flow.say: Bottle A has 100 millilitres of water. This is the standard. The other five have a little more, from 110 up to 160. Put a secret letter on each base, so the lifter cannot tell. Close the caps tight.
flow.kid: Fill bottle A with 100 millilitres. Fill the others a little more. Close the caps tight.
flow.parent: The bottles must look the same and feel the same on the outside. The helper keeps the key and does not tell the lifter. If you have fewer than six bottles, use two or three and add water between rounds with the jug.
flow.context: In this step, you fill the bottles for the light set. The lifter does not see which bottle has how much.

flow.do: Blindfold the lifter and sit them down. Give them the standard in one hand and the bottle with 110 millilitres in the other. Ask which is heavier. Swap hands at random, and repeat 4 times. Then move on to 120, 130, 140 and 160.
flow.say: Hold this bottle in one hand and this one in the other. Which is heavier? Tell me the hand. Do not lift them high, just a little. Now again with the hands swapped, and another bottle.
flow.kid: Hold two bottles. Say which is heavier. We swap hands and try again.
flow.parent: Put the heavier bottle in the right hand on some tries and the left on others, in a mixed order, so a lifter cannot just guess the same hand. Write R for right and W for wrong. The smallest extra that the lifter always got right, together with the next one up, is the answer. If they get 110 right every time, try 105 and 102 as well.

check.q: Why does the helper put the heavier bottle in a different hand each time?
options: So the lifter cannot get it right by always picking the same hand
So the bottles stay full
So the lifter does not get tired
check.why: If the heavier bottle were always in the right hand, the lifter could just say 'right' and score full marks. Mixing the hands means that only feeling the weight can give a correct score.

flow.context: In this step, you test the light set, from the smallest extra up to the biggest.

flow.do: Empty the bottles. Fill the standard with 400 millilitres. Fill the others with 440, 480, 520, 560 and 640 millilitres. Put new secret letters. Repeat the lifting test in the same way.
flow.say: Now the heavy set. The standard has 400 millilitres. The others have 40, 80, 120, 160 and 240 more. These steps are four times bigger than before, so we can compare fairly. Lift and tell me which is heavier.
flow.kid: Fill A with 400 millilitres. Fill the others with more. Do the same test.
flow.parent: The extras are four times the light-set extras, so each is the same share of its standard. The standard has four times as much water. The empty bottle also has a small weight, so the shares will not match exactly. Wipe any spilled water. If the lifter always gets 440 right, try 420 and 410 as well. All the numbers here are typical, not promised, and a few lifters will feel much smaller or larger steps.
flow.context: In this step, you do the same test again with heavier bottles.

flow.do: For each set, find the smallest extra that was always right. Divide it by the standard and multiply by 100 to get the share. Ask your child for their claim, their evidence and their reasoning before you explain anything.
flow.say: Look at the smallest extra you always got right in each set. Divide that extra by the standard bottle. Multiply by 100 to get a share out of 100. What do you notice? What is your claim? What is your evidence? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Find the smallest extra you got right each time. Compare the two sets.

ask.q: Was the extra the same in both sets? Was the share the same?
good: The extra in millilitres was bigger for the heavy set, but the share was about the same.
The heavy set needed 4 times as much water.
The share out of 100 was about 10 to 20 in both.

flow.parent: Typical result: the lifter needs an extra of about 10 to 20 millilitres for the light set and about 40 to 80 for the heavy set. The share is about 10 to 20 out of 100 for both. If your results differ, write them as they are and, if you can, test again. Do not explain Weber's law yet. Let the child say what they found.

check.q: A lifter needs an extra of 20 millilitres on a 100 millilitre bottle. About how much extra would they need on a 400 millilitre bottle if the share stays the same?
options: About 80 millilitres
About 20 millilitres
About 4 millilitres
check.why: 20 out of 100 is the share. The same share of 400 is 80, because 400 is four times as much as 100 and 20 times 4 is 80. Picking 20 means expecting the extra to stay the same whatever the weight.

flow.context: In this step, you turn the extra water into a share and compare the two sets.

activities.title: The Tired Nose: how fast does a smell fade, and how fast does the nose wake up?

materials.item: a small steel katori holding 1 to 2 teaspoons of crushed cloves, cardamom or saunf (fennel seeds); an adult crushes them
a strip of orange or lemon peel, as a second smell
a clock, phone or kitchen timer that shows seconds
paper and a pencil, to write a table with times and scores from 0 to 5
a window or balcony with fresh air
a helper to keep time

activities.safety: Check for food allergies and asthma first. Hold the katori about 10 centimetres from the nose and breathe normally. Never sniff hard. If anyone has a blocked or sore nose, use only the orange peel. Keep the crushed spice away from eyes and do not taste it. Keep the katori away from small brothers and sisters, who may put it in their mouths.

schedule.what: Guess. Smell until the smell fades and time it. Rest in fresh air and test again at 30 seconds, 1 minute and 3 minutes. Try the second smell. Write what you found. With 2 to 4 children, test one child at a time. The others wait in another room, since the smell lingers and tires their noses too. Roles: smeller, timer, writer.

activities.record: Write how many seconds it took for the first smell to fade. Then write a score from 0 to 5 for the smell at 30 seconds, 1 minute and 3 minutes after the rest. Write the score for the second smell right after the first had faded.
activities.context: In this activity, you hold a strong smell near your nose until it fades. Then you time how long your nose takes to wake up, and find out whether a second smell fades too.

setup.art: A child sitting at a table with a steel katori of spices held about ten centimetres below the nose, and a helper with a timer beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the katori about 10 centimetres from your nose. The helper starts the timer.

setup.art: The child raising a hand as the smell fades, and the helper writing the time in a table.
setup.caption: 2. Raise your hand when the smell is almost gone. The helper writes down the seconds.

setup.art: The child standing at an open window breathing fresh air while the helper holds the timer.
setup.caption: 3. Rest by the window. Then smell again after 30 seconds, 1 minute and 3 minutes.

setup.art: A strip of orange peel being held under the nose right after the spice smell had faded.
setup.caption: 4. Right after the first smell fades, smell the orange peel. Does it fade too?

flow.do: Show your child the katori of spices and the orange peel. Ask for a guess and a reason about how long the smell will last. Write the guess on the table.
flow.say: I will hold this spice a hand's width from your nose. You will tell me when the smell has almost gone. How long will that take? Will a second smell fade too? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How long until the smell fades? Will a new smell fade too? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a smell might fade when it is still there?
good: My nose gets used to it.
The smell gets used up.
I stop paying attention to it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A common idea is that the smell runs out. The test can show that it does not.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tired Nose activity. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Hold the katori about 10 centimetres from your child's nose and start the timer. Your child breathes normally and raises a hand when the smell is almost gone. Write the number of seconds.
flow.say: Breathe normally. Tell me what you smell. Raise your hand when it is almost gone. I will watch the clock.
flow.kid: Breathe normally. Raise a hand when the smell is almost gone.
flow.parent: Most people say the smell fades within about 30 seconds to 2 minutes. If nothing fades after 3 minutes, stop and say so. That is a real result. Keep the katori at the same distance, and do not let the nose touch it. If the spice is too faint to start with, crush it more or hold it 5 centimetres away. If the smell does not fade in 3 minutes, try orange peel as the first smell instead. Compare two children's fade times only as a fun fact, because noses and distances differ.

check.q: The smell has almost gone. The cloves are still in the katori. What has changed?
options: The nose is reporting the smell less
The cloves have run out of smell
The smell has moved to the other room
check.why: The cloves are still giving off the smell. The receptors in the nose have adapted, and send fewer pulses. A child who picks 'run out' is thinking of the smell as a thing that gets used up. The next steps can test this.

flow.context: In this step, you time how long it takes for the smell to fade.

flow.do: Take the katori away. Your child rests by the open window. After 30 seconds, hold the katori to the nose again and score the smell from 0 to 5. Repeat after 1 minute and after 3 minutes. Write the scores.
flow.say: Come to the window and breathe the fresh air. After half a minute I will hold the spice again. Tell me how strong it is, from nothing to very strong.
flow.kid: Rest at the window. Smell the spice again after a while. Give it a score.
flow.parent: Typical, not promised: the smell is weak after 30 seconds, stronger after 1 minute and nearly full after 3 minutes. The nose recovers in a few minutes. The numbers may vary, so write what you find.
flow.context: In this step, you let the nose rest and test how fast it recovers.

flow.do: Make the first smell fade again. Right after it fades, hold the orange peel to the nose and score the orange smell from 0 to 5.
flow.say: Let us fade the spice again. As soon as it is gone, smell this orange peel. How strong is the orange? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Fade the spice again. Then smell the orange. How strong is it?
flow.parent: Expected: the orange smells strong straight away. The nose adapts to one smell, not to every smell. If the orange also seems weak, the child may simply be tired. Try again after a rest.

check.q: The orange smells strong right after the spice smell faded. What does that suggest?
options: Smell receptors adapt to one smell at a time
The brain has stopped working
The orange is stronger than the spice
check.why: The receptors that detect clove molecules were tired. The receptors that detect orange molecules were not. So adaptation is specific to the smell, which is why a newcomer's smell in a room still stands out.

flow.context: In this step, you test whether a second smell fades too.

flow.do: Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning. Then ask them where in their home they have stopped noticing a smell, and who could be a fresh nose.
flow.say: What is your claim about a smell that stays the same? What did you measure? Why do you think it happened? Where at home might you have stopped noticing a smell?
flow.kid: What happened to the smell? What did you measure? Why did it happen?

ask.q: Why might it be useful for the nose to fade a steady smell?
good: It lets the nose notice new smells.
It saves effort.
I would not want to smell my own clothes all day.

flow.context: In this step, you say what you found and link it to your own home.

activities.title: The Rubber Hand: can your eyes fool your skin?

materials.item: a rubber kitchen glove, stuffed with cotton wool or crumpled newspaper so that it looks like a hand
two soft paintbrushes of the same size (any soft brushes, such as makeup or small art brushes)
a stiff piece of cardboard about 40 by 30 centimetres, from a carton, to stand up as a screen
a small towel or a dupatta to cover the glove's wrist and the real arm, so the glove looks like it is joined to the arm
a table and a chair
a clock with seconds, and a paper and pencil to record scores from 0 to 5. The pencil is also used for the gentle tap

activities.safety: Only soft brushes and a rubber glove are used. If anyone has a latex allergy, use a cloth or non-latex glove. The grown-up must not hit the glove hard. Only a gentle tap with a pencil, if the child agrees, is allowed. Stop if the child feels uneasy. The feeling is harmless and goes away within a few seconds. With several children, only one child sits behind the screen at a time.

schedule.what: Guess. Set up the screen and the glove. Stroke both together for 2 minutes and score. Stroke out of time for 2 minutes and score. Write what you found.

activities.record: Write a score from 0 to 5 for 'how much the rubber hand feels like mine' after the matched round and after the out-of-time round. Write what you felt.
activities.context: In this activity, you see a rubber hand being stroked while your real hand is hidden and stroked in the same way. You find out whether your brain starts to treat the rubber hand as yours.

setup.art: A child sitting at a table with the left arm resting behind a cardboard screen and a rubber glove lying in front in a natural position about 15 centimetres to the side, covered at the wrist by a cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Put the real hand behind the screen. Put the rubber glove in front, with the wrist covered by the cloth.

setup.art: A helper holding two paintbrushes and stroking the child's hidden index finger and the same finger of the glove at exactly the same time.
setup.caption: 2. The helper strokes the same finger of both hands at the same time for two minutes. The child watches the glove.

setup.art: The same child and helper, but this time the brushes are moving at different times, one stroking and one resting.
setup.caption: 3. Try again, with the strokes out of time with each other. Compare.

flow.do: Show the glove, the screen and the brushes. Explain that you will stroke a hidden hand and a rubber hand. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Your real hand will be behind this screen. You will look at this rubber hand while I stroke both with a brush. What do you think you will feel? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will look at a rubber hand. A brush strokes it and your real hand. What will you feel?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the feeling of the stroke on your hidden hand?
good: I will feel it in my real hand only.
I might feel it in the rubber hand.
I do not know.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say they will feel only their real hand. It is fine to be surprised.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubber Hand activity. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Sit your child at the table. Rest their left hand and forearm behind the screen, out of sight. Put the glove about 15 centimetres to the side of where the hidden hand is. Cover the glove's wrist and the child's sleeve with the cloth so it looks joined.
flow.say: Rest your left hand behind the screen. Keep looking at the rubber hand in front. Try not to look at anything else. I will cover the wrist so the hand looks joined to your arm.
flow.kid: Put your hand behind the screen. Look at the rubber hand. Keep your eyes on it.
flow.parent: The child's real hand and the glove must be in the same position, both with palms down. The child must not see their own hand. Put the glove close enough that it looks like the child's own.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the screen and the rubber hand.

flow.do: Take a brush in each hand. Stroke the hidden index finger and the same glove finger at the same moment, once each second, for two minutes. Ask 'where do you feel the touch?' at 30 seconds and 2 minutes. Score from 0 to 5.
flow.say: Keep looking at the rubber hand. I will stroke your hidden finger and the rubber finger together. Where do you feel the touch? How much does the rubber hand feel like yours, from nothing to very much?
flow.kid: Watch the rubber hand. Say where you feel the touch. Give a score.
flow.parent: The two brushes must move in step, at the same speed and the same place. Most people, but not all, start to feel the touch in the rubber hand within about a minute. If your child feels nothing, that is a normal result, so write down 0. About 6 to 8 in 10 people feel it, and it may take longer than a minute. With 2 to 4 children, one is the subject, two stroke (one brush each, practising to stay in step), and one keeps the clock and scores. Rotate. For a measurement, before and after each round, the subject shuts their eyes and slides the other index finger along the table edge to touch their hidden finger. Mark the spot with tape and measure how far it moved toward the rubber hand.

check.q: Your child says the rubber hand 'feels like mine'. What is the best explanation?
options: The brain matched what it saw with what it felt, and guessed that the rubber hand is part of the body
The glove is really joined to the arm
The brush has magic in it
check.why: The eyes saw a brush touching the rubber hand while the skin felt a touch at the same moment. The brain looked for the best explanation and picked the visible hand. It is a guess, and it can be wrong. Picking 'joined' or 'magic' ignores that the real hand was behind the screen.

flow.context: In this step, you stroke both hands together and score how much the rubber hand feels like yours.

flow.do: Rest for a minute. Now stroke the hidden finger and the glove's finger at different times, for two minutes. Score again. Then, if your child agrees, tap the glove gently with a pencil and watch for a flinch.
flow.say: Now I will stroke them out of step. Keep looking at the rubber hand. What do you feel this time? Give a score. At the end, I may tap the glove once. Tell me if you would rather I did not.
flow.kid: Now the strokes are out of step. Watch the glove. Give a new score.
flow.parent: Out-of-time strokes usually give a much lower score, which shows that the matching in time is what makes the feeling. If the child jumps when the glove is tapped, the brain treated the glove as a part of the body. Never hit the glove hard.
flow.context: In this step, you stroke out of time and compare the score with the matched round.

flow.do: Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning. Then ask how this connects to a person who has lost a hand and still feels it.
flow.say: What is your claim? What did you feel in each round? Why do you think matched strokes made the difference? What does this tell you about how the brain decides which hand is yours?
flow.kid: Which round felt most like your hand? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What does this tell you about how the brain decides which body parts belong to you?
good: It uses what it sees and what it feels together.
It makes a best guess.
The feeling of owning a hand can be changed.

flow.context: In this step, you say what you found and link it to how the brain builds a body.

activities.title: Bouba or Kiki: do sounds have shapes?

materials.item: two sheets of plain paper and a thick black pen
at least 10 people to ask, from children to grandparents, who speak the languages of your home or street
a tally sheet with two columns: 'bouba is the round one' and 'bouba is the spiky one'
a pencil

schedule.what: Guess. Draw the two shapes. Ask at least 10 people one by one and tally. Add up and find the share out of 100. With 2 to 4 children, each child asks their own 5 people, and you pool the tallies.

activities.record: Tally how many people said 'bouba' is the round shape and how many said 'bouba' is the spiky shape. Work out how many in every 10 chose round.
activities.context: In this activity, you ask people which of two shapes is called 'bouba' and which is called 'kiki'. You find out whether sounds seem to go with shapes.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper side by side, one with a soft round cloud shape and one with a sharp spiky star, each with no name on it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw one soft round shape and one sharp spiky shape. Do not name them.

setup.art: A child showing both sheets to a grandmother and asking which is bouba and which is kiki.
setup.caption: 2. Show both shapes to one person at a time. Ask which one is 'bouba' and which is 'kiki'.

setup.art: A tally sheet with two columns and a row of small tick marks being added up.
setup.caption: 3. Tick the tally for each person. Add up at the end.

flow.do: Tell your child that two made-up words, 'bouba' and 'kiki', are names for two shapes. Ask for a guess and a reason about which word goes with which shape.
flow.say: These two words are made up. They do not mean anything. Which shape do you think is called 'bouba', the round one or the spiky one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two made-up words. Bouba and kiki. Which shape is bouba? Why?

ask.q: What makes you pick that word for that shape?
good: Bouba sounds soft and round.
Kiki sounds sharp and pointy.
I say it with my mouth and it feels that way.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say that 'bouba' is the round one. Do not tell the child that this is what most people say until the test is over.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bouba or Kiki test. You guess before you ask people.

flow.do: Draw a soft, round, cloud-like shape on one sheet and a sharp, spiky, star-like shape on the other. Make them about the same size. Do not write any names on them.
flow.say: Draw one soft round shape and one sharp spiky shape. Make them about the same size. Do not put names on them.
flow.kid: Draw a soft round shape. Draw a spiky shape. Make them the same size.
flow.parent: Keep the shapes clear and simple. If one is much bigger, people may pick by size.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the two shapes.

flow.do: Show both shapes to one person at a time. Ask them which is 'bouba' and which is 'kiki'. Do not give a hint. Put a tick in the right column. Swap which sheet is on the left for every other person.
flow.say: Here are two shapes. One is called bouba and one is called kiki. Which is which? Go with the first feeling.
flow.kid: Show the shapes. Ask which is bouba. Tick the tally.
flow.parent: Swap the sheets' positions for every other person, so that left and right do not matter. Ask different ages and people who speak other languages, if you can. Do not discuss the answer until you have asked everyone. Say the two words the same way each time and never say 'round' or 'spiky'. Ask people one at a time, out of hearing of the next. If you cannot find 10 people, use a phone call or ask over two days, because fewer than 10 tell very little.

check.q: Why do we swap which sheet is on the left for every other person?
options: So that left or right does not change the answer
So the paper stays clean
So people have to think harder
check.why: Some people may tend to pick the left one. If the round shape were always on the left, you could not tell whether people chose by sound or by position. Swapping balances this out.

flow.context: In this step, you ask at least 10 people one by one and tally their answers.

flow.do: Add up the tally. Work out how many people in every 10 said that 'bouba' is the round shape. Compare with your guess.
flow.say: Let us add up the ticks. How many said bouba is the round one? How many in every 10 is that? Does it match your guess? What is your claim? What is your evidence?
flow.kid: Count the ticks. How many said bouba is round? Did most agree?

ask.q: What would it mean if most people picked round for 'bouba'?
good: Sounds and shapes seem to match for many people.
It is not random.
Different senses are linked in the brain.

flow.parent: Expected: most people, in many languages, say bouba is round. A few will pick the other way, and that is fine. Scientists found much the same in the USA and in India in 2001. No one knows exactly why. One idea is that the mouth shape for 'bouba' is round and soft, and for 'kiki' is sharp and tight.
flow.context: In this step, you add up your results and compare them with your guess.

projects.title: The Reaction Ruler: build a ruler that reads time, and hold a three-day family league

materials.item: a strip of stiff cardboard about 5 centimetres wide and 35 centimetres long (from a carton)
a 30 centimetre ruler, a pencil and a thick marker
a sheet of paper to write the distance-to-time guide and the league table
2 or more family members as catchers (3 or more is better) and one dropper; a parent and child can swap jobs

schedule.what: Make the Reaction Ruler. Test each family member in the morning, 7 catches each.
Test the same people after lunch or in the evening. Do 7 catches each.
Test again while each person counts backwards from 100 in sevens. Draw the league table and write your findings.

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the cardboard strip with scissors. The catcher sits down and the ruler is light, so a miss hurts no one.
projects.record: A league table with each person's middle value for each of the three tests, in centimetres and in seconds. A short note on what you found.
projects.context: In this project, you make a ruler that shows reaction time directly in seconds, and use it to test your family at different times of the day and while distracted.

setup.art: A cardboard strip on a table with a ruler beside it, and marks being made every 5 centimetres from the bottom with the times 0.10, 0.14, 0.17, 0.20, 0.23 and 0.25 written beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the cardboard strip every 5 centimetres from the bottom. Write the time next to each mark.

setup.art: A grandfather catching the cardboard ruler between thumb and finger while a child holds the top, ready to drop it.
setup.caption: 2. Test each family member with the same drop method as in the Ruler Drop test.

setup.art: A table with three columns for morning, evening and distracted, and a name down the side of each row, filled in with numbers.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in the league table for three tests.

flow.do: Show your child the cardboard strip. Explain that it will show reaction time in seconds, after the distance guide. Ask for a guess about what changes the time.
flow.say: We will make a ruler that shows your reaction time directly. Then we will test the whole family. Do you think a person is faster in the morning or in the evening? Is a person slower when their mind is busy? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We make a ruler that shows time. Who is fastest? Does time of day matter? Why?

ask.q: What do you think might make a person faster or slower?
good: Being sleepy makes you slower.
Being busy thinking about something else makes you slower.
Practice makes you faster.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Reaction Ruler project. You guess before you build and test.

flow.do: Mark the cardboard strip at the bottom as 0. Use the ruler to make marks every 5 centimetres. Write the times beside the marks. 5 cm is 0.10 seconds. 10 cm is 0.14. 15 cm is 0.17. 20 cm is 0.20. 25 cm is 0.23. 30 cm is 0.25.
flow.say: Draw a line at the bottom for zero. Mark every 5 centimetres going up. Write the time beside each mark. A thing that falls a short way took a short time. A thing that falls further took longer.
flow.kid: Mark the strip every 5 centimetres. Write the time beside each mark.
flow.parent: These times come from the way things fall: the time for a fall of d metres is the square root of 2d divided by 9.8, rounded. You do not need to explain this yet. The time gaps between the marks get smaller further up the strip, which shows that the time grows more slowly than the distance.

check.q: On the strip, the gap between 0.10 and 0.14 seconds is 5 centimetres, but the gap between 0.23 and 0.25 seconds is also 5 centimetres. What does that tell you?
options: A falling ruler speeds up, so each extra centimetre takes less time further down
The marks were drawn wrongly
The ruler is falling at the same speed all the way
check.why: A falling thing speeds up. Near the top it moves slowly, so 5 centimetres takes a lot of time. Further down it is moving faster, so the same 5 centimetres takes less time. Equal gaps in distance do not mean equal gaps in time.

flow.context: In this step, you make the Reaction Ruler and add the time marks.

flow.do: On day 1, test each family member in the morning. The dropper holds the strip at the top. The catcher keeps thumb and finger open at the 0 end. Do 3 practice tries and then 7 counted tries. Write the middle value.
flow.say: Rest your arm on the table. Watch the strip. I will drop it without warning. Catch it as fast as you can. Seven counted tries. We will take the middle one.
flow.kid: Rest your arm. Watch the strip. Catch it when it drops.
flow.parent: Test everyone at about the same time of day. Use the same method as in the Ruler Drop test. Write each person's middle value in centimetres and then read the time off the strip. If the cardboard strip flutters, fold it along its length or tape a second strip behind it. With 2 to 4 children, one drops, one writes and the rest catch in turn.
flow.context: In this step, you test each family member on day 1.

flow.do: On day 2, test everyone again, but at a different time of day, for example after lunch or in the evening. Use the same method. Write the middle values.
flow.say: Today we test again at a different time of day. Same method, same rules. Are you faster or slower than yesterday? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Test again at a new time of day. Are you faster or slower?
flow.wait: Do this on day 2, at a different time of day from day 1.
flow.parent: Results may be close, or noisy. If the numbers are about the same, that is a real result. Tiredness, hunger and mood can change reaction time, but only by a small amount.
flow.context: In this step, you test the same family members at a different time of day.

flow.do: On day 3, test everyone while they count backwards from 100 in sevens. Then draw the league table and ask for the claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Today you must catch the strip while counting backwards from 100 in sevens, out loud. What do you think will happen to your time? Then we will look at all three tests together and see who was fastest, and what changed.
flow.kid: Count backwards from 100 in sevens. Catch the strip too. Is it harder?

ask.q: Why might a busy mind slow down a reaction?
good: The brain has to do two jobs at once.
The decision to move waits for the counting.
Attention is shared and not all of it goes to the strip.

flow.parent: Expected: most people are slower when distracted, often by a few centimetres. Draw the league table with a row for each person and a column for each test. Do not turn it into a contest about who is best, because reaction times change with the day. If counting back in sevens is too hard for your child, use threes. It should be hard but possible.

check.q: A person catches the strip at 14 cm normally and 19 cm while counting backwards. About how much longer was the second time?
options: About 0.03 seconds longer, from about 0.17 to 0.20 seconds
About 0.5 seconds longer
There was no change
check.why: 14 centimetres is about 0.17 seconds and 19 centimetres is about 0.20 seconds on the strip. The difference is about 0.03 seconds. Small, but it counts. A longer distance means a longer reaction time.

flow.context: In this step, you test while the catcher is distracted and finish the league table.

challenges.title: Pulse Talk: send a message using only touch
challenges.problem: Send the five-word message 'PLEASE BRING ME A BOOK' from one person to another using only taps on the back of the hand. The receiver has their eyes shut and their ears covered. Get all the letters right in under six minutes.
constraints: No speaking, no humming, no sounds and no signs the receiver could see.
Only taps, pressure, or strokes on the back of the receiver's hand may be used.
The receiver must write down every letter they think they received.
You may agree on your code beforehand, but you cannot change it once the message has started.
All taps must be gentle, so nobody is hurt.
materials: a pencil and paper for the code and the receiver's writing
a clock or timer with seconds
a blindfold or a cloth, and soft earplugs or cotton wool for the receiver
a table to rest the hands on
general: A tap code that counts taps for each letter, one tap for A, two for B, and so on. It is simple and slow.
A grid code: write the alphabet in a 5 by 5 grid, and tap the row number, pause, then the column number for each letter.
Short and long taps like Morse code, with a pause between letters and a longer pause between words.
A code that only taps for the most common letters, and spells the rest out.
creative: Use six fingers or six spots on the hand as the six dots of a Braille cell, and tap the dots that make up each letter.
Use how hard the tap is as part of the code, soft and hard, so each tap carries two kinds of information.
Agree on short signs for common words like 'please', 'a' and 'me', to cut the time down.
Use pairs of taps in a rhythm, so the receiver recognises rhythms and not only counts taps.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own code on paper. Test it on a short word like 'TEA'. Change one thing, such as how long you pause. Then send the whole message and time it. Which design was fastest with no mistakes? Why do you think it worked?
challenges.safety: Do not push cotton wool or earplugs deep into the ear. Hold soft ear covers or earmuffs over the ears instead. Taps stay gentle.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about signals. The nerves of your senses only send pulses, so you try to build a code that works with pulses alone.

setup.art: Two children sitting at a table, one with a cloth over the eyes and cotton wool in the ears, and the other tapping the back of their hand.
setup.caption: 1. The receiver sits with eyes shut and ears covered. The sender taps on the back of the receiver's hand.

setup.art: A paper with a 5 by 5 grid of letters on it, and two numbers beside a letter, showing a row and a column.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your code on paper before you start. A grid code uses a row number and a column number.

setup.art: A timer showing six minutes and the receiver writing letters on a paper.
setup.caption: 3. Send the message and time it. The receiver writes down each letter.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to draw two or three different code ideas on paper.
flow.say: You have to send a whole message with only taps on a hand. How could you turn letters into taps? Draw some ideas before you try them.
flow.kid: Send letters with taps only. Draw two ideas for a code.

ask.q: What can a tap change to carry more information?
good: How many taps.
How long the pause is.
How hard the tap is.
Which finger or spot is tapped.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Pulse Talk challenge. You plan your code.

flow.do: Choose one code. Write it on paper. Practise sending the word 'TEA' and the word 'BOOK'. Swap roles and practise again.
flow.say: Choose the code you want to try. Write it down so you both know it. Then practise on the words 'TEA' and 'BOOK'. Swap roles so both of you can send and receive.
flow.kid: Pick one code. Write it down. Practise a short word. Then swap roles.
flow.parent: Practise with the receiver's eyes shut and ears covered, so the practice is as hard as the real test. If the first code feels too slow, do not give up. Slowness is a clue about what to change.
flow.context: In this step, you pick a code and practise on short words.

flow.do: Send the full message. Start the timer. The receiver writes every letter. When it ends, check the letters and the time.
flow.say: Now send PLEASE BRING ME A BOOK. The receiver writes down every letter. Keep your taps gentle and steady. When you finish, we will check the time and the mistakes.
flow.kid: Send the whole message. Receiver, write each letter. Check the time.
flow.parent: Count the number of wrong letters as well as the time. A fast message with many mistakes is not a success. Try to find where the mistakes started: was it a pause, a missed tap or a mix-up in the code?

check.q: Why does a code that uses only taps still work, even though a tap carries so little information?
options: Patterns of taps in time and place can stand for many different letters
A tap can hold a whole word
The receiver can guess the message
check.why: A single tap says almost nothing. But the number of taps, the pauses and the place can be combined into many different patterns. Your nerves work the same way: pulses of equal size carry information by their timing and by which thread they travel on.

flow.context: In this step, you send the full message and time it.

flow.do: Change one thing in your code. Send the message again, or a new five-word message, and compare the time and the number of mistakes.
flow.say: Pick one thing to change. Maybe the length of the pause, or the order of the code. Send again. Is it faster or slower? Are there more or fewer mistakes?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Send again. Was it faster? Were there fewer mistakes?

ask.q: What did you change, and why did it help or not help?
good: A shorter pause made it faster but caused more mistakes.
Using the grid code made fewer mistakes.
The fastest code was not the clearest one.

flow.context: In this step, you improve your code and test again.

flow.do: Ask your child which code worked best. Then ask how it is like the way senses send pulses to the brain.
flow.say: Which code was the best? How is sending a message with taps like the way your skin sends signals to your brain? What is the same? What is different?
flow.kid: Which code worked best? How is it like a nerve sending pulses?

ask.q: How is a tap code like the way nerves send messages?
good: Both use many pulses of the same size.
Both use timing and place to carry meaning.
A receiver has to decode the pulses.

flow.context: In this step, you link your code to how nerves carry messages.

items.p: A harder press on your skin makes a touch nerve do what?
opts: Send a different kind of pulse
items.why: All nerve pulses are the same size. A stronger stimulus makes more of them each second. Picking 'bigger pulses' is a common idea, because we imagine a signal like a loud sound, but a pulse is either there or not there.

items.p: The smallest amount of a stimulus that a sense can notice is called the ____.
items.why: A threshold is the faintest amount that a sense can pick up. Anything below it goes unnoticed.

items.p: Light travels so fast that you can catch a dropped ruler with no delay inside your body. True or false?
items.why: False. The light reaches your eye almost at once, but the signal has to travel to the brain, a decision has to be made, and a signal has to travel to your hand. That takes about a fifth of a second.

items.p: Which steps are part of your reaction time when you catch a falling ruler?
opts: Only the time the ruler takes to fall
The signal going to the brain, a decision, and the signal going out to the hand
Only the time your hand takes to close
Only the time light takes to reach your eye
items.why: Your reaction time is the whole chain from the stimulus to the movement. A child who picks 'only the hand' forgets the signal travelling in and the deciding.

items.p: Put the steps of catching a falling ruler in order: fingers close, signal travels down the arm, eye notices the ruler move, brain decides to catch, signal reaches the brain.
items.why: The eye notices first. The signal goes to the brain, which decides. Then a new signal goes out along the arm to the muscles, and the fingers close. Every step takes time.
items.art: A child watching a ruler fall, with five small circles joined by arrows from the eye up to the brain and down the arm to the fingers.

items.p: Match each kind of nerve thread to the job it does.
pairs: Wrapped thread, about 100 metres each second
Telling the brain where your muscles are
Wrapped thread, about 50 metres each second
Medium thread, about 15 metres each second
Thin unwrapped thread, about 1 metre each second
items.why: Jobs that need an answer fast, like keeping your balance, use fast wrapped threads. Slow, aching pain uses thin unwrapped ones.

items.p: After you stub your toe, a sharp pain comes first and a deep ache comes a moment later. What is the best reason?
opts: Two kinds of nerve thread carry the pain at different speeds
The toe hurts twice because it is hit twice
The brain has to think about the ache first
The ache is made in the toe, and the sharp pain is made in the head
items.why: Fast threads bring the sharp pain and slow threads bring the ache. Both reach the brain, but at different times. Picking 'hit twice' ignores that the threads have different speeds.

items.p: When a smell stays the same for a long time, the smell receptors ____ and send fewer pulses.
items.why: Adaptation is when a sense reports a steady stimulus less and less. The nose still gets the smell, but the signal fades.

items.p: A visitor walks into your home and says it smells of fried onions. You cannot smell it. Why?
opts: Your smell receptors have adapted to the smell and theirs have not
The visitor has a stronger nose
The smell is only in the visitor's mind
items.why: Receptors fade a steady smell. Your nose has been in it for hours, so the signal has faded. A visitor's receptors are fresh. Picking 'broken' misses that every nose does this.

items.p: The brain has pain nerves, so brain surgery on an awake patient must hurt a great deal. True or false?
items.why: False. The brain tissue itself has no pain receptors. Surgeons can work on an awake patient with only the scalp numbed. Pain is made by the brain, but it is not felt in the brain tissue.

items.p: On the brain's body map, the lips and fingertips take up a very large patch. Why?
opts: They are the strongest parts of the body
They are closest to the brain
They are the oldest parts of the body
items.why: The brain gives more room to parts that send more detailed signals. Lips and fingertips are packed with receptors. Size of patch follows detail, not strength or distance.

items.p: Sort these into things that fade from notice if they stay the same, and things that do not fade much.
items: the hum of a ceiling fan
the smell of frying onions in your own kitchen
the pain of a thorn in your foot
the feel of clothes on your shoulders
items.why: Touch, sound and smell adapt, so steady ones fade. Pain adapts much less, because a warning that faded while you were still being hurt would be dangerous.

items.p: Why can you not tickle yourself?
opts: Your brain predicts your own touch from your movement and turns the feeling down
Your skin is less sensitive to your own fingers
You get used to it too fast
items.why: When you move your own finger, your brain knows what touch to expect. It turns down that expected signal. A touch you did not make cannot be predicted, so it stays strong.

items.p: A friend says: 'My eyes show me the world exactly as it is, right now.' Write two reasons from the science of the senses for why this is not quite true.
items.a: Signals take time to travel from the eyes to the brain and to be sorted, so what we see is a fraction of a second old. The brain also guesses and fills in parts of the picture, so it is a build, not a copy.
items.why: A strong answer gives at least two reasons, such as the delay in signals, the brain's predictions or the filling in of gaps. The best answers say that the experience is still very useful.

items.p: Explain to a younger child why it is good that your nose stops noticing the smell of your own house.
items.a: If your nose reported the same smell all day, you would not notice a new smell, such as smoke or something burning. By fading steady smells, your nose is ready to tell you about changes.
items.why: A strong answer says that fading frees the sense to notice new things, and gives an example of a change that matters, such as smoke or a gas leak.

items.p: Draw a nerve thread with three pulses for a light touch and ten pulses for a hard press. Label which is which.
items.a: Two threads of the same length. The first has three small identical sparks along it, labelled light touch. The second has ten identical sparks, labelled hard press. The sparks are all the same size.
items.why: A strong drawing shows pulses of equal size, with more of them for the stronger stimulus.
items.art: Two empty horizontal threads running from a fingertip on the left to a brain on the right, with space to draw sparks.

worksheets.title: Thresholds, Ratios and the Guessing Brain (stretch)

items.p: A person can just tell 100 grams from 110 grams. About how much would the same person need to add to a 500 gram weight to just feel the difference?
items.why: 10 out of 100 is the fraction. The same fraction of 500 grams is 50 grams. Picking 10 grams expects the extra to stay the same, which is not how the sense works.

items.p: Why is it harder to hear a whisper in a noisy market than in a quiet library?
opts: The noise raises the amount of extra sound you need to notice anything new
Your ears get tired in a market
items.why: A whisper is a small change on top of the noise. Because the change you can notice is a fraction of what is already there, the noise hides it.

items.p: A stronger touch makes a nerve send more ____ each second, not bigger ones.
items.why: The strength of a stimulus is coded in the number of pulses each second.

items.p: A person who walks from bright sunshine into a dark hall will see as well after ten seconds as after twenty minutes. True or false?
items.why: False. The light cells in the eye take time to become sensitive. Cones recover in minutes and rods need about 20 to 30 minutes to be fully ready.

items.p: A signal on a fast pain thread goes at 15 metres each second. The path from the toe to the brain is about 1.5 metres. About how long does the signal take?
items.why: Time is distance divided by speed. 1.5 divided by 15 is 0.1. A child who picks 1 second has used the speed of the slow thread.

items.p: A sprinter starts 0.08 seconds after the gun. Why is that counted as a false start?
opts: Reaction times that fast are not possible, so the runner must have guessed the gun
The sound of the gun was not loud enough
Sprinters must wait for a flash, not a sound
items.why: The signal has to go from the ear to the brain and back to the legs, and that takes more than a tenth of a second. A faster start means the runner did not wait for the sound.

items.p: Sort each story by the idea that explains it.
items: You stop feeling your watch after a few minutes
You cannot see a candle's light in bright sunshine
The smell of mustard oil fades in your own kitchen
You stumble on a step that is not there
An extra 20 grams on a 2 kilogram sack is not felt
items.why: A steady thing that fades is adaptation. A change that is too small next to what is there is a ratio matter. Something that the brain expected is a guess.

items.p: Put these nerve threads in order from the fastest signal to the slowest: slow dull pain, sharp pain, touch, muscle position.
items.why: Big wrapped threads are fastest, at about 100 metres each second for muscle position and 50 for touch. Sharp pain is about 15 and slow pain about 1.
items.art: Four runners at a starting line labelled with the four kinds of nerve thread.

items.p: Match each animal to a sense that humans lack.
pairs: Sensing the electric field around a flower
items.why: Each animal has receptors for something that we have no receptors for. Their senses are built for the life they live.

items.p: A person who lost a hand feels a touch on their cheek as a touch on their missing fingers. What is the best explanation?
opts: The cheek patch and the hand patch lie side by side on the brain's body map, and signals from the cheek spread into the hand patch
The cheek has become part of the hand
items.why: The brain's map is real and the hand's patch is still there. When it gets no signals, its neighbour can spread into it. The feeling is real. Picking 'imagining' misses that it can be tested.

items.p: A friend says pain is a direct measure of how damaged the body is. Give two pieces of evidence against this.
items.a: People with a phantom limb feel pain from a limb that is no longer there. A person born without pain nerve gates feels no pain from broken bones. A paper cut can hurt more than a bigger bruise.
items.why: Strong answers show that pain is made by the brain from danger signals and context. Evidence can include phantom limbs, people who feel no pain, and soldiers or players who notice a wound only later.

items.p: A mantis shrimp has 12 to 16 kinds of colour receptor, yet was no better than people at telling similar colours apart. What does this show?
opts: More kinds of receptor do not automatically give finer colour vision
People have the most receptors of any animal
items.why: Having many kinds of receptor is not the same as comparing colours finely. How the signals are used matters too. Picking 'colour blind' goes too far, because the shrimp can clearly sense colours.

items.p: If a picture is held perfectly still on the retina, you see it more and more clearly. True or false?
items.why: False. A picture held perfectly still on the retina fades within seconds. The tiny movements of the eyes keep the picture alive.

items.p: Is the world you experience the real world? People who study the senses give different answers.

views.says: When I look at a mango, I see the mango itself. A delay of a fifth of a second does not change what I see.

views.who: A neuroscientist who studies the predicting brain
views.says: My brain builds a best guess from late signals, then checks it. The mango I experience is that guess.

views.who: A teacher of Advaita Vedanta, an Indian school of thought
views.says: The shapes and colours of the senses are appearance. The one awareness behind them is what is real.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing, and what from the science of the senses supports your choice?
items.a: Any view is fine if the reason uses what the senses do, such as the delay in signals, adaptation or prediction.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names a view, uses evidence from the unit, such as signal delay, the rubber hand or the bee's colours, and says what would change their mind.

items.p: Label the three stages of catching a falling ruler on the picture: 'signal goes in', 'brain decides', 'signal goes out'.
a: eye to brain: signal goes in
brain to hand: signal goes out
items.why: The reaction has three parts. The signal goes in from the eye. The brain decides. A signal goes out to the muscles of the hand.
items.art: A child's head and arm in outline, with the eye, the brain and the hand marked by empty boxes joined by arrows.

items.p: Draw two bags in a child's hands, one light and one heavy. Show how much extra weight is needed to feel a difference in each.
items.a: A small bag with a small extra and a big bag with a bigger extra, in the same share. For example, 10 grams on a 100 gram bag and 100 grams on a 1 kilogram bag.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the extra needed grows with the starting weight, in about the same fraction.
items.art: Two children's hands, one holding a small cloth bag and one holding a much larger bag, with empty space to draw the extra weight.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether your reaction time is slower when you are talking. Say what you would keep the same and what you would change.
items.a: I would catch a dropped ruler seven times while sitting quietly and seven times while talking. I would use the same ruler, the same hand and the same dropper, and change only whether I am talking. Then I would compare the middle values.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing, here talking, and keeps the rest the same. Strong answers use repeated tries and a middle value.

items.p: A touch signal at 50 metres each second and a slow pain signal at 1 metre each second both start in a toe 1.5 metres from the brain. About how much later does the pain signal arrive?
items.why: The touch signal takes about 0.03 seconds and the pain signal takes 1.5 seconds. The difference is about 1.5 seconds. Picking 'at the same time' forgets that the threads have different speeds.

items.p: A cyclist rides at 5 metres each second. Her reaction time is 0.2 seconds. How far does she go before she even starts to brake?
items.why: Distance is speed times time. 5 times 0.2 is 1 metre. Any reaction time means you travel some distance before you can respond, which is why we keep a gap between us and the vehicle in front.

items.p: A ruler caught after falling 20 centimetres means a reaction time of about ____ seconds.
items.why: A thing that falls 20 centimetres takes about 0.2 seconds. This comes from the way things speed up as they fall.

items.p: A catch distance of 10 centimetres means a reaction time half as long as a catch distance of 20 centimetres. True or false?
items.why: False. 10 centimetres is about 0.14 seconds and 20 centimetres is about 0.20 seconds. Because a falling thing speeds up, doubling the distance does not double the time.

items.p: Meera can just feel a 5 gram change in a 50 gram parcel. Using the same fraction, about how big a change must there be in a 400 gram parcel?
items.why: 5 out of 50 is one tenth. One tenth of 400 grams is 40 grams. Picking 5 expects the same amount of change to work for any weight.

items.p: Why does the eye respond to ratios of brightness instead of fixed steps?
opts: So it can work in dim starlight and in bright sunshine, a range of billions of times, without being dazzled
So all colours look the same
So it can ignore moving things
items.why: A sense that responded to fixed steps would be dazzled in daylight or blind in starlight. Working in ratios squeezes a huge range into one that the nerves can handle.

items.p: On the decibel scale, every step up of 10 means the sound energy is ____ times as much.
items.why: Decibels use ratios, as our hearing does. Ten steps up means ten times the energy, yet it sounds only about twice as loud.

items.p: Match each nerve thread to how long a signal needs to go 1.5 metres.
pairs: Muscle position thread, 100 metres each second
Sharp pain thread, 15 metres each second
Slow pain thread, 1 metre each second
items.why: Time is distance divided by speed. 1.5 divided by 100 is 0.015, divided by 50 is 0.03, divided by 15 is 0.1 and divided by 1 is 1.5.

items.p: In a silent room at night, you can hear your own heartbeat. In the daytime you cannot. Has your heartbeat changed?
opts: No. The daytime noise raises the amount of sound you need to notice anything
Yes, it is quieter by day
Yes, ears work better at night
No. Heartbeats are only heard at night
items.why: The sound of the heart is the same. Daytime noises make a small sound a tiny change on top of a lot of noise, so you cannot notice it.

items.p: When a rubber hand and a hidden hand are stroked out of step, most people feel nothing special about the rubber hand. What does that show?
opts: The feeling needs the sight and the touch to match in time
The rubber hand is too heavy
items.why: When the touch and the sight match, the brain's best guess is that the hand it can see is yours. Out of step, the guess fails.

items.p: A friend says: 'Plants cannot sense anything because they have no brain.' Using what you know about pulses, write a reply.
items.a: Sensing does not need a brain. A Venus flytrap uses electrical pulses, and counts two touches within about 20 seconds before she closes. Plants sense light, touch and chemicals, and they respond.
items.why: A strong answer uses a plant example, such as the Venus flytrap counting pulses, and says that sensing means detecting and responding, which plants do.

items.p: A cook who has been in a smelly kitchen all day is more likely to miss a gas leak than someone who has just walked in. True or false?
items.why: True. The cook's smell receptors have adapted and send fewer pulses. A newcomer's receptors are fresh. That is why you should step outside and come back in if you suspect a smell.

items.p: Should a sense show what is true, or what is useful? Scientists give different answers.

views.who: Donald Hoffman, a scientist in the USA
views.says: Evolution rewards senses that help us survive, not senses that show the truth. Our colours and shapes are like icons on a screen, useful and not true.
Senses that show the world wrongly would lead animals to bad mistakes. Useful senses must be close to the truth in the ways that matter.
A bee sees patterns on flowers that I cannot. For her those patterns are the flower, and they guide her to the nectar.

items.ask: Is a bee's view of a flower true, useful, both or neither? Give a reason.
items.a: Any view is fine if the reason uses what the senses do. A good answer might say that a bee's colours are true to the light that reaches her, and useful for finding nectar.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer separates the question of truth from the question of use, and gives a reason.

items.p: Draw a timeline of a falling ruler: when it starts to fall, when the light reaches the eye, when the signal reaches the brain and when the fingers close. Mark which gap is longest.
items.a: A line with four marks in order. The first two marks are almost at the same place because light is very fast. The signal reaches the brain a little later. The fingers close last. The longest gap is from the eye or brain to the fingers closing.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that light is almost instant and that most of the delay is inside the body.
items.art: A long horizontal line with a ruler dropping at the left end and a hand closing at the right end, and empty space for marks.

items.p: Label this drawing of the brain's body map: which patch is big and which is small? Lips, back, hand.
items.why: Parts with many receptors, like lips and hands, get big patches. The back has few receptors close together, and gets a small patch.
items.art: A strip of brain with three arrows pointing to patches of different sizes, with empty label boxes.

items.p: Two astronomers time the same star and differ by 0.8 seconds. Describe how to find out whether one made a mistake or each simply has a different delay.
items.a: Have both of them time the same event many times, such as a clock hand or a light that flashes at known moments. If each is steady but they differ by the same amount each time, each has a different delay. If the gap changes a lot, someone is making mistakes.
items.why: A strong answer repeats the measurements and uses an event with a known time, then compares the pattern of differences.

quiz.p: Which is the best description of a nerve pulse?
opts: A tiny wave of electricity that is always the same size
A small drop of liquid that carries light
A bigger spark for a stronger touch
A picture sent to the brain
quiz.why: All pulses are the same size. A stronger stimulus gives more of them each second. Picking 'a bigger spark' mixes up the size with the number.

quiz.p: A very bright light shines in your eye. What do the nerves from the eye do?
opts: Send the light to the brain
quiz.why: A stronger stimulus makes more pulses each second. The light never reaches the brain. Only the pulses do.

quiz.p: When you catch a falling ruler, where is most of the delay between the ruler starting to fall and your fingers closing?
opts: Inside your body: the signal going in, the decision and the signal going out
In the light travelling to your eye
quiz.why: Light takes almost no time. The delay is the time for signals to travel and for the brain to decide. A child who picks 'the light' has not yet separated the world from the body.

quiz.p: In simple reaction tests, how do sight, hearing and touch usually compare?
opts: Touch and hearing are usually slightly quicker than sight
All three are exactly the same
quiz.why: The eye does extra work before it sends its signal, so sight is usually a little slower. The differences are small, about a hundredth to a few hundredths of a second.

quiz.p: Which kind of nerve thread carries a signal fastest?
opts: A thick one wrapped in myelin
A thin one with no wrapping
quiz.why: Myelin works like the plastic around a wire. Signals jump along wrapped threads and are much faster. Length and temperature matter less.

quiz.p: A hearing test finds the softest beep you can just hear. What is that level called?
quiz.why: A threshold is the smallest amount of a stimulus that a sense can notice. A ratio is a comparison. Adaptation is fading. Reaction time is a delay.

quiz.p: Someone can just feel an extra 100 grams on a 1 kilogram weight. About how much extra do they need on a 3 kilogram weight, if the fraction is the same?
quiz.why: 100 grams out of 1000 is one tenth. One tenth of 3000 grams is 300 grams.

quiz.p: Why do you stop noticing a perfume that you wear all day?
opts: Your smell receptors adapt and send fewer pulses
The perfume wears off your skin
You grow tired of the shop
quiz.why: The perfume is still on your skin, but a steady smell fades. Other people, whose receptors are fresh, can still smell it.

quiz.p: If you drew the body as the brain's body map shows it, what would it look like?
opts: Huge lips, hands and tongue and a tiny back
A big head and tiny arms
A tiny hand and huge legs
quiz.why: Parts with many receptors get big patches on the brain's map. Lips, hands and the tongue are packed with them. The back has few.

quiz.p: A person who lost a hand feels itching in the missing fingers. Where is that feeling made?
opts: In the brain's patch for the hand
In the air where the hand used to be
quiz.why: The brain's patch for the hand is still active. The feeling is real as a feeling, and it is made in the brain.

quiz.p: You step down onto a stair that is lower than you expected, and you jolt. What happened?
opts: Your brain predicted a stair at a different height
quiz.why: The brain predicts what the foot will meet and prepares the leg. A surprise tells you the prediction was wrong.

quiz.p: Which animal can sense the weak electric fields of other animals?
quiz.why: Sharks have jelly-filled pores on their snout that sense weak electric fields. The platypus does something similar. Many animals have senses we do not.

applications: Hearing tests that find the softest sound each ear can notice, so that hearing problems are found early.
Setting safe following distances for vehicles, because every driver has a reaction time during which the vehicle keeps moving.
Starting guns and false-start rules in running races, which depend on the shortest possible human reaction time.
Sensory substitution devices that let blind people feel a picture with the skin or the tongue.
Mirror therapy for people with phantom limb pain, which uses sight to calm the brain's map of the missing limb.
Adding a strong smell to cooking gas so that a leak is noticed even at very low amounts.
Decibel and star-magnitude scales, which use ratios because the senses work in ratios.
Screens that change their brightness to the room's light, so that the eye's changes are comfortable.
Tea tasting, spice grading and perfume making, where years of practice train the brain to read fine differences.
Eye tests and hearing tests that measure thresholds with repeated questions and a middle value.

open_questions.q: How does the brain make one steady 'now' from signals that arrive at different times?
open_questions.why_open: Sight, sound and touch take different times to arrive and be sorted. Scientists have clues, such as the brain waiting briefly for the slowest signal, but nobody has a full account.

open_questions.q: Why do some people feel the rubber hand as their own, and others do not?
open_questions.why_open: The test works on most people but not all. Scientists are still studying what is different about the people it does not work on.

open_questions.q: Can people sense the Earth's magnetic field without knowing it?
open_questions.why_open: A 2019 test saw changes in brain waves when the field turned. Other scientists want it repeated, and no one knows if it changes what we do.

open_questions.q: How exactly do birds sense magnetism?
open_questions.why_open: One idea is a special molecule in the eye. Another is tiny iron crystals in the beak. Both have some evidence and neither is settled.

open_questions.q: What is it like to feel the electric field of a hidden fish, as a shark does?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what the receptors detect. We cannot measure what the shark experiences, and nobody has a way yet.

open_questions.q: How does a pattern of pulses in the brain become the feeling of pain, or the taste of a mango?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can follow the pulses a long way. Why they feel like anything is still an open question, sometimes called the hard problem.

maths.problem: Meena caught the ruler seven times. The distances in centimetres were 14, 17, 12, 16, 15, 19 and 13. Put them in order and find the middle one. About what reaction time does the middle one show, if 15 centimetres is about 0.17 seconds?
maths.answer: The middle one is 15 centimetres, which is about 0.17 seconds.
maths.explain: In order, the numbers are 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19. The fourth number is 15, so it is in the middle. The guide says 15 centimetres is about 0.17 seconds.
maths.context: In the Ruler Drop test, you catch a falling ruler seven times and use the middle value.
maths.why_maths: A middle value is not changed by one lucky or sleepy try, so it is a fairer way to sum up a set of tries.

maths.problem: Farah caught the ruler at 10 centimetres. Meena caught it at 20 centimetres. Farah says, 'My reaction time was half of yours.' About 10 centimetres is 0.14 seconds and 20 centimetres is 0.20 seconds. Is Farah right?
maths.answer: No. Her time was about 0.14 seconds and Meena's was about 0.20, so hers was not half as long.
maths.explain: Half of 0.20 is 0.10. Farah's time was 0.14, which is more than 0.10. The distance was half, but the time was not, because a falling ruler speeds up. So equal steps in distance are not equal steps in time.
maths.context: In the Ruler Drop test, the distance the ruler falls is turned into a reaction time.
maths.why_maths: It shows why you must not assume that half the distance means half the time, and so you should check a claim with the numbers.

maths.problem: A touch signal goes from a toe to the brain, 1.2 metres, at 60 metres each second. A slow pain signal goes the same way at 1 metre each second. How long does each take? How many times as long is the slow one?
maths.answer: The touch signal takes 0.02 seconds. The slow pain signal takes 1.2 seconds. The slow one takes 60 times as long.
maths.explain: Time is distance divided by speed. 1.2 divided by 60 is 0.02. 1.2 divided by 1 is 1.2. 1.2 divided by 0.02 is 60, which matches the 60 times difference in speed.
maths.context: Nerve signals travel at very different speeds, from about 1 to 100 metres each second.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a distance by a speed tells you how long a signal takes, and it explains why a stubbed toe hurts twice.

maths.problem: A person can just feel an extra 15 millilitres of water on a 100 millilitre bottle. If the share stays the same, how much extra will they need on a 400 millilitre bottle? What about a 1 litre bottle?
maths.answer: 60 millilitres on the 400 millilitre bottle, and 150 millilitres on the 1 litre bottle.
maths.explain: 15 out of 100 is the share. 400 is 4 times 100, so the extra is 4 times 15, which is 60. 1 litre is 1000 millilitres, which is 10 times 100, so the extra is 10 times 15, which is 150.
maths.context: In the Bottle Lift test, you find the smallest extra water you can feel on a light and on a heavy bottle.
maths.why_maths: Scaling the same share up to a heavier bottle lets you predict a result before you test it.

maths.problem: In a Bottle Lift test, a lifter needed an extra of 20 millilitres on a 100 millilitre bottle and an extra of 60 millilitres on a 400 millilitre bottle. Which extra was the bigger share of its standard? What does that suggest?
maths.answer: The light bottle needed 20 out of every 100 and the heavy bottle needed 15 out of every 100. The light bottle needed the bigger share, so this lifter was a little better with the heavy bottle.
maths.explain: 20 divided by 100 is 0.20, or 20 out of every 100. 60 divided by 400 is 0.15, or 15 out of every 100. The shares are close, but not equal. Weber's law is only approximate, so small differences like this are normal.
maths.context: In the Bottle Lift test, the extra water is turned into a share of the standard bottle.
maths.why_maths: A share lets you compare a small bottle and a big bottle fairly, which the plain number of millilitres cannot do.

maths.problem: An auto goes at 36 kilometres each hour, which is 10 metres each second. The driver's reaction time is 0.25 seconds. How far does the auto go before the driver starts to brake? What if the auto goes twice as fast?
maths.answer: 2.5 metres at 10 metres each second, and 5 metres at 20 metres each second.
maths.explain: Distance is speed times time. 10 times 0.25 is 2.5. At twice the speed, 20 times 0.25 is 5. Twice as fast means twice as far before the driver even starts to brake.
maths.context: Every reaction time is a delay during which a moving thing keeps moving.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying speed by reaction time shows why vehicles need a gap, and why going faster needs a bigger one.

maths.problem: Meena scored the smell of a spice from 0 to 5. Right after it faded, the score was 0. After resting 30 seconds the score was 1, after 60 seconds it was 2 and after 180 seconds it was 4. Her brother says the score goes up by the same amount each minute. Is he right?
maths.answer: No. In the first minute the score rose by 2. In the next two minutes it rose by only 2 in total, which is 1 each minute. The nose wakes up quickly at first and then more slowly.
maths.explain: From 0 to 60 seconds the score went from 0 to 2, a rise of 2 in one minute. From 60 to 180 seconds it went from 2 to 4, a rise of only 1 each minute. So the recovery is faster at first and slower later. A line graph of these scores would bend and not be straight.
maths.context: In the Tired Nose activity, you score the smell after resting for different times.
maths.why_maths: Reading the steepness of a line graph shows whether something changes at the same rate or not.

maths.problem: In a Bouba or Kiki test, 17 out of 20 people said that 'bouba' is the round shape. If people were just guessing, about how many out of 20 would you expect to say round? How many more than that said round? How many out of every 100 is that?
maths.answer: About 10 out of 20. 7 more than guessing. 17 out of 20 is 85 out of every 100.
maths.explain: A random guess between two shapes would give about half, or 10 out of 20. 17 minus 10 is 7. 17 out of 20 is the same as 85 out of 100, because 20 times 5 is 100 and 17 times 5 is 85.
maths.context: In the Bouba or Kiki activity, you ask people which shape fits which word.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a result with what guessing would give tells you whether the result means something.

maths.problem: Each eye sends about 1 000 000 nerve threads to the brain. A signal from the eye needs about 0.1 seconds to reach the brain. How many threads do two eyes send? If the brain gets 10 pulses each second from every thread, how many pulses arrive each second?
maths.answer: Two eyes send 2 000 000 threads. At 10 pulses each second, that is 20 000 000 pulses each second.
maths.explain: 1 000 000 times 2 is 2 000 000. 2 000 000 times 10 is 20 000 000. The 0.1 second time is not needed for this answer. It is extra information.
maths.context: Every sense sends the brain streams of pulses, and the eyes send the most.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying big numbers shows how much information the brain handles every second, and why sorting it takes time.

The Class 3 unit on the five senses, which this unit builds on. It showed that every sense sends nerve signals. This unit asks how long they take, how big a change must be, why steady things fade and how the brain guesses.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Ruler Drop: a light plastic ruler and a table edge are enough. The catcher's arm rests on the table, the 0 mark is level with the top of the thumb, and the dropper waits a different time each go. Differences between sight, sound and touch are small, usually 1 to 3 centimetres, so the steps use seven counted tries, a middle value and a reversed order, and say that equal results are a real result. Bottle Lift: six identical 1-litre bottles and a measuring cup are enough. Lifters often get the 10 percent step right, and the steps say to try smaller extras if so. Tired Nose: use a mild spice at 10 centimetres and never sniff hard. Check for allergies and asthma first. The fade time varies a lot from person to person. Rubber Hand: it works for most people but not all, and the steps say that 'nothing' is a normal result. Bouba or Kiki: ask at least 10 people and swap the sheets' sides. Pulse Talk: the grid code is slow but accurate, and the steps tell the parent to count mistakes as well as time. Facts to verify before release: the 1850 Helmholtz speed of about 30 metres each second (it has been quoted between about 25 and 43); Müller's claim that the speed could not be measured; the speeds of the pain and touch threads, which are rounded; the Hecht result of fewer than 15 caught light particles; the 1998 Blakemore tickle test details; the 2013 bumblebee electric-field study; the 2000 ferret study by von Melchner, Pallas and Sur; and the Bouba and Kiki result with Tamil speakers from 2001. Numbers that are not certain are marked 'about' or 'reported'. The videos are still to be chosen.

quiz: Your reaction is never instant, because signals take time to travel and your brain takes time to decide.
A signal goes in, the brain decides, and a signal goes out, and each step takes time.
A stronger light makes a nerve send more pulses each second, not bigger pulses.
Every nerve pulse is the same size, so strength is written in how often they come.
A very faint stimulus can be there and still not be noticed.
Below the threshold, a sense is too weak to notice the stimulus.
You cannot tickle yourself because your brain predicts the touch from your own movement.
The brain turns down signals it expected, so your own touch feels much less ticklish.
Practice can sharpen a sense, as tea tasters learn to tell very small differences in flavour.
Practice changes how the brain uses the signals, so a trained sense can notice more.
You see and hear things at the very moment they happen.
Signals take time to reach the brain and be sorted, so what you sense is already a little old.
A small added weight is as easy to feel on a heavy bag as on a light one.
The smallest change you notice is a fraction of what was there, so a heavy load hides small changes.
Pain tells you exactly how much damage your body has taken.
Pain is a warning the brain makes. A small paper cut can hurt a lot, and a bad wound may hurt little.
An animal with more kinds of colour receptor must tell close colours apart better.
Mantis shrimps have many kinds, yet they were worse than people at telling close colours apart.
A smell fades while you stand in it because the smell itself gets weaker.
The smell stays the same, but your receptors and brain report a steady smell less and less.
odd: The first three are senses many animals have that humans lack a receptor for; humans do taste sweet.
The first three take real time and make up the reaction delay; light reaches the eye almost at once.
The first three stay steady, so your senses adapt and notice them less; a clap is a sudden change.
Lips, fingertips and tongue have many receptors and big patches in the brain's body map; the back has few.
The first three are parts of the system that carries signals; bone does not carry nerve signals.
